ELSE/rand.dev.body: Use [rand.dev] to generate random numbers that deviate within a given range. If only one 'x' float is given as an argument or via the right inlet, then the range is input-x, input+x. If you have a 'x, y' list input via the argument or inlet, then the range is input+x, input+y.

title: rand.dist

methods.description: a float sets seed, no float sets a unique internal

ELSE/rand.dist.body: [rand.dist] is an abstraction based on [array quantile] and generates random numbers that follow a probability density function (given by an array). A float input (like from an external random source) outputs the array quantile instead. The first argument is the table name containing the probability density function. The output range is from 0 to 127 by default, but you can change that with the 2nd and 3rd argument or the 2nd or 3rd inlet. The output resolution is the range divided by the table maximum index, so a 128-point table with the default 0-127 range outputs integers.

title: rand.f

set number of elements to output

ELSE/rand.f.body: [rand.f] generates random float values for a given range when triggered with a bang. Use the seed message if you want a reproducible output.

title: rand.f~

methods.description: a float sets seed, no float sets a unique internal

ELSE/rand.f~.body: [rand.f~] generates random float values for a given range when triggered. A trigger happens at positive to negative or negative to positive transitions. Use the seed message if you want a reproducible output.

ELSE/rand.hist.body: [rand.hist] generates weighted random numbers based on a histogram, which specifies how many times an index is output: with 3 2 5, index 0 has a 30% chance of occurring, 1 has 20% and 2 has 50%. A list sets a new histogram. In "unrepeat" mode, a random sequence is output without repetition, where 3 2 gives index 0 three times and index 1 twice. When the sequence is finished, a bang comes out the right outlet, and the 'restart' message clears the memory so you can start a new sequence.

ELSE/resonant~.body: [resonant~] is a bandpass resonator filter like [bandpass~], but it doesn't have a maximum dB value of 0, so changing the Q increases the gain of the filter. Besides 'Q' and 'bw' you can also set the resonance as 't60' (like with [resonator~]).

title: resonator2~
ELSE/resonator2~.body: [resonator2~] is a wrap around [cpole~]. It is very similar to [vcf~], which is also a wrap around [cpole~], but has no constant maximum gain at 0dB - so it works like [resonator~] with a constant skirt. Like [resonator~], it takes a decay time for resonance. Unlike [resonant~], you shouldn't excite it with noise as the filter produces very high gain output, so it's really suited just to be excited by impulses. By the way, this filter is the basis of [damp.osc~] and [resonbank2~].

title: resonator~
ELSE/resonator~.body: [resonator~] is just like [resonant~], but the resonance parameter is defined as resonance time in 't60'. It has 3 modes, the default is bandpass, which is like [resonant~], then you can also have lowpass (like [lowpass~]) and highpass (you guessed it, like [highpass~]). Note that a t60 value of 0 bypasses the input! For a bank of [resonator~] objects, see [resonbank~]. For another similar filter, see [resonator2~].

ELSE/resonbank2~.body: [resonbank2~] is a bank of resonators made of [resonator2~] objects. The design and structure here is different than [resonator2~] in order to make it better suited for sound synthesis. It has the same design as [resonbank~] and has a list of partials for each resonator and a frequency multiplier in the left inlet, kinda like [oscbank~]. The mid inlet the trigger (or excitation) signal (kinda like [pluck~]) - this must be an impulse since noise sources and noise bursts generate very loud outputs! The rightmost inlet is a time multiplier for the decay times. The number of filters is set via the parameter list size (such as the partial list). There's also support for multichannel output.

ELSE/route2.body: [route2] is similar to route, but it doesn't trim the list selector and always outputs messages with a proper selector. Another difference is that you can mix floats and symbols as arguments. Each argument creates a corresponding outlet and there's an extra rightmost outlet for messages that don't match the arguments.

title: routeall

messages.description: any message to be routed completely
the input message, at each outlet whose argument it matches

arguments.description: arguments to match the 1st element of a message

ELSE/routeall.body:
[routeall] routes messages and - unlike [route] - keeps its first element! Also differently from [route], the [routeall] object matches a symbol to a symbol or a list message! Another difference is that [routeall] takes both float and symbol messages at once! Moreover, it can match to other elements in the message than the first.
Each argument has its corresponding outlet. The object searches for a match between the first element of a message and an argument (from first to last). As soon as a match is found, it sends the message to the corresponding output - this means that it stops looking for other matches. If no match is found, the message is sent to the rightmost outlet.

[routetype] routes messages according to its type, such as "bang", "float", "list" and "symbol". There is also the "anything" type, which is can be defined as "any other" message that is not the former ones.
These 5 types are given as arguments, and there's an outlet corresponding to each given argument that sends out the message type according to the arguments(bang", "float", "list", "symbol" or "any").

ELSE/seq.m~.body: [seq.m~] is a MERDA step sequencer module with up to 16 steps per page, and several pages for concatenated sequences, each with its own BPM, beat multiplier and number of steps. Its outlets send MIDI pitch, a gate lasting half a beat, an impulse at each step and the internal clock. The left inlet runs the sequencer with a gate, and the others take impulses for an external clock and to reset to the first step.

Symbol elements are sent without a symbol selector (and can be note names or anything else). A "bang" comes out as a proper "bang".

If you slice at 'n', the left outlet spits the first 'n' elements and the right outlet sends the remaining elements. If the number of channels is less than the split point, the whole signal is output to the left if 'n' is positive (and the right outlet outputs zeros), and to the right if negative (and the left outlet outputs zeros).

title: vca2~

ELSE/vca2~.body: [vca2~] is a stereo voltage controlled amplifier with two inputs and outputs and a CV input, the basis of the [vca2.m~] module. It sums multichannel inputs into a single channel by default, has a master gain, and outputs levels to feed [vu] objects.

title: vca~

methods.description: nonzero sum polyphonic (MC) channels into a single one

ELSE/vca~.body: [vca~] is a mono (one in/out) VCA. It is the basis of the [vca.m~] MERDA module. For convenience, it sums polyphonic (multichannel connections) inputs into a single channel by default. You also have a general gain compensation and a right output to feed a [vu] object. Yeah, not much different than just using [*~].

title: vcf.m~

messages.description: MIDI pitch for keyboard tracking of the cutoff

ELSE/vcf.m~.body: [vcf.m~] is a MERDA voltage controlled filter module with multichannel input and controls for cutoff, resonance and drive. The CV inputs go through attenuverters and add to the knob values, and the right inlet takes MIDI pitch for keyboard tracking. The cutoff spans 10 octaves, from about 16 Hz to 16 kHz.

title: vco.m~
ELSE/vco.m~.body: [vco.m~] is a MERDA voltage controlled oscillator module with a polyphonic MIDI pitch input (60 when nothing is connected) and CV inputs for frequency modulation, phase modulation and pulse width modulation (for the square and variable saw shapes), plus a sync input that takes impulses. A detune number box shifts the pitch in Hz, and a transposition knob by up to 3 octaves.

title: velvet~

methods.description: a float sets seed, no float sets a unique internal

ELSE/velvet~.body: [velvet~] is a velvet noise generator, which randomly chooses either positive (1) or negative (-1) impulses at random positions in a given period set in Hz. A polarity bias is possible to set the amount of positive and negative impulses. A time regularity parameter forces a impulses with less randomness. An amplitude irregularity forces random values (different than 1 or -1). The object has support for multichannel.

title: vibrato~
ELSE/vibrato~.body: [vibrato~] is a pitch shifter abstraction with an LFO controlling the pitch deviation in cents.

title: vocoder~

messages.description: list of frequencies (in MIDI) for each channel

arguments.description: List of frequency (in MIDI) for each channel
arguments.default: equally dividing the range in MIDI from 28 and 108 for the number of channels

methods.description: list of frequency (in MIDI) for each channel

ELSE/vocoder~.body: [vocoder~] is classic cross synthesis channel vocoder abstraction.

ELSE/voices.body: [voices] is used to implement polyphonic synths. It's like Pd Vanilla's [poly] object, but with more functionalities. By default, it routes the voices to different outlets, but it also has a list mode similar to [poly].

title: voices~

messages.description: MIDI note messages (note and velocity pair or more)

methods.description: sets number of voices (in list mode only)

ELSE/voices~.body: [voices~] is an abstraction based on [voices] and generates multichannel signals that can be used to control pitch and gate with polyphony.

title: vosim~
ELSE/vosim~.body: [vosim~] implements a VOSIM synthesis algorithm. This is an oscillator that you specify the fundamental (f0) frequency and the center (or formant) frequency (both parameters in Hz). This technique is used to synthesize vocal sounds. The object has support for multichannels.

ELSE/vu~.body: [vu~] combines [rms~] and [peak~] to provide dBFs output to Pd Vanilla's [vu] GUI.

ELSE/xmod~.body: [xmod~] performs cross modulation of two sine oscillators. It can perform either frequency (default) or phase modulation.

Gem/GEMglTexImage2D.body: [GEMglTexImage2D] calls glTexImage2D() each time a gemlist passes through it, with the parameters set by its creation arguments and inlets. The image is the pix in the gemlist; its format, type and data go to the call as they are. Gem passes its inlets to glTexImage2D shifted by one: the one named xoffset sets the internal format, yoffset the width, width the height and height the border. See glTexImage2D in the OpenGL reference.

An impulse is a single sample with a value of one followed by zeros, and this is the default impulse generated by [click~], but you can can also an impulse with a different amplitude value or even as a list of values (for band limited impulses - maximum is 256 sample values).

It has a negative maximum delta for when the signal decays and a positive maximum delta for when it rises. When they're both 0, the signal doesn't shift. When used in a FFT subpatch, it can keep a running phase deviation of the FFT because the FFT size is equal to the block size.

title: number~

sets display time interval in ms

cyclone/number~.body:
Use [number~] to monitor or generate signals. This is an abstraction with limited functionality, not a proper clone.
The "tilde" symbol refers to monitor mode, and if you click on it, it changes to generator mode (marked with a down arrow, where you can click/drag and enter numbers). Clicking on the arrow switches it to monitor mode.

cyclone/offer.body: [offer] stores a x/y integer number pair and accesses the 'y' value from the corresponding 'x' (after retrieving, the pair is deleted).

title: onepole~
cyclone/onepole~.body:
Similar to Pd vanilla's [lop~], [onepole~] implements the simplest of IIR filters, providing a 6dB per octave attenuation.
This filter is very efficient and useful for gently rolling off harsh high end and for smoothing out control signals.

title: overdrive~
cyclone/overdrive~.body:
[overdrive~] simulates the "soft clipping" of and overdriven tube-based circuit by applying a non-linear transfer function to the incoming signal.
If the "drive factor" is 1, the signal is unchanged. Increasing the "drive" increases the amount of distortion. If the "drive" is less than 1, then it causes a different kind of distortion. If the "drive" is less than 0, VERY LOUD distortion can result, so be careful (here we use [clip~])!

title: pak

cyclone/past.body: [past] bangs when an input is greater than a threshold value and the last value was below or equal to it. The input needs to fall back to a value equal or below the threshold for another bang to be output when it goes past it again.

[peak] compares the input to a 'peak' (maximum) value. If it's greater, the input becomes the new peak and is sent out. The middle outlet sends 1 when a new peak is set and 0 otherwise. The right outlet sends 1 when the input is not greater than the peak and 0 otherwise.
Note: In Pd, [peak] only deals with floats, not ints.

title: peakamp~

cyclone/peakamp~.body: Use the [peakamp~] object to report the absolute value of the peak amplitude of a signal since the last time it was reported. It outputs the peak amplitude when banged or via its own internal clock.

title: phaseshift~

messages.description: signal whose phase will be shifted
sets the frequency that is shifted by 180 degrees

cyclone/phaseshift~.body: [phaseshift~] is a 2nd order allpass filter: it keeps the gain and only shifts the phase, from 0 (at 0 Hz) to 360 degrees (at the Nyquist frequency). The frequency that is shifted by 180 degrees is the filter's frequency, and the Q parameter sets how steep the curve is. Adding the shifted signal to the original cancels frequencies by phase opposition.

title: phasewrap~
cyclone/phasewrap~.body: Use [phasewrap~] to wrap the input between pi and -pi, which is useful for wrapping phase values. When the input exceeds pi (about 3.14159), the output wraps around to -pi (about -3.14159).

title: cyclone/pink~

methods.description: a float sets seed, no float sets a unique internal

cyclone/pink~.body: [pink~] generates pink noise. This is not an actual MAX clone but an object that is borrowed from ELSE which has more functionalities and is backwards compatible to MAX's object since the original just outputs pink noise! White noise has constant spectral power, but pink noise has constant power per octave and it decrease 3dB per octave.

cyclone/play~.body: [play~] plays any part of an array, it can play at different speeds (with interpolation) and backwards. It may also loop with optional crossfading. The interpolation is the same as [tabread4~]'s.

[plusequals~] or [+=~] accumulates the received values. Each input sample is added to the previous ones for a running sum. So, started at 0, a signal consisting of 1 values outputs the sequence (1, 2, 3, 4, etc...).
The internal sum can be reset to 0 with a bang (left inlet) or a signal different than 0 in the right inlet (with sample accuracy) - or also set to any value (with the set message).

[round] approximates positive and negative numbers to an integer multiple of any given number that is greater or equal to 0 (0 makes no approximation - so the original input is output unchanged).
It works in two modes, rounding to the nearest multiple (default) or to the approximating to the truncated multiple value.

This usually synchronizes one signal to the behavior of another.

messages.description: to be combined into a list with another input close in time
time interval for combining items to a list
list of elements stored within a time interval

cyclone/thresh.body: [thresh] collects numbers and lists into a single list if they come within a certain given amount of time. Each item or list is appended to the previous stored items. The time count is reset at each incoming item.

title: thresh~

messages.description: a signal whose level you want to detect

cyclone/thresh~.body:
[thresh~] is a "Schmitt trigger". When the input is greater than or equal to the high threshold level, the output is 1 and becomes 0 when the signal is equal to or less than the reset level (low threshold).
If low and high threshold are the same, the output is 1 until a sample in the input signal is less than the reset level (thus it works in the same way as [>=~]).

title: togedge

messages.description: switches the stored value between 0 and nonzero
if a zero to nonzero transition is detected
if a nonzero to zero transition is detected

cyclone/togedge.body: [togedge] sends a bang in the left outlet for "zero to nonzero" transitions, and a bang in the right outlet for "nonzero to zero" transitions.

title: tosymbol
cyclone/tosymbol.body: [tosymbol] converts any kind of message to a symbol message (maximum of 2048 characters).

title: train~
cyclone/train~.body:
[train~] generates a pulse signal alternating from on (1) to off (0) at a period given in ms. It also sends a bang when going from 0 to 1, so it can be used as a metronome.
A pulse width of 0 has the smallest "on" pulse size (a single sample), while a pulse width of 1 has the largest (the entire period except the last sample). The "onset phase" delays the "on" portion by a fraction of the total pulse period.

title: trapezoid~
cyclone/trapezoid~.body:
[trapezoid~] is a trapezoidal wavetable that is read with phase values from 0 to 1 into the first inlet- a [phasor~] input turns it into a wavetable oscillator. A second and third inlet change the position of ramp up/down points.
The default lo/hi values are 0 and 1, but may be changed using the lo/hi messages or attributes to any given range.

title: triangle~

messages.description: the triangle wavetable output based on args

cyclone/triangle~.body:
[triangle~] is a triangular wavetable that is read with phase values from 0 to 1 into the first inlet- a [phasor~] input turns it into a wavetable oscillator.
A second inlet changes the position of the peak value (variable duty, from 0 to 1), going from sawtooth like waveforms to triangular ones.
The default lo/hi points are -1 and 1, but may be changed using the lo/hi messages to any given range.

title: trough
cyclone/trough.description: output numbers smaller than the previous

messages.description: a value to be compared with the trough value
2nd number sets new 'trough', then 1st element is input
1 (input is a new trough) / 0 (input is not a new trough)
1 (input is not a new trough) / 0 (input is a new trough)

cyclone/trough.body:
[trough] compares the input to a 'trough' (minimum) value. If it's smaller, the input becomes the new trough and is sent out. The middle outlet sends 1 when a new trough is set and 0 otherwise. The right outlet sends 1 when the input is not smaller than the trough and 0 otherwise.
Note: In Pd, [trough] only deals with floats, not ints.

title: universal
cyclone/universal.description: sends messages to all objects of the same type

messages.description: sends any message to an object type

methods.description: sends any message to an object type

cyclone/universal.body: [universal] sends messages to all instances of the same object in a patch and/or in a subpatch window.

title: unjoin
cyclone/unjoin.description: break a list into separate messages

messages.description: message to split into groups of elements
the list composed of the joined messages

cyclone/unjoin.body: [unjoin] separates a list's elements by groups of any size (default 1). Each group is sent out a separate outlet, extra elements are sent to an extra outlet.

title: urn

messages.description: clears the memory and sets size
bangs if all numbers have been generated

methods.description: clears the memory (the list of already generated numbers)

cyclone/urn.body: [urn] generates random numbers in a range defined by the 'n' size (from 0 to n-1) without repeating them. When all numbers have been output, a bang is sent to the right outlet and it stops generating numbers unless it receives a clear message.

title: uzi

messages.description: set number of bangs and start the loop
bang according to the counter loop
bangs after the last bang in the loop has fired

cyclone/uzi.body: [uzi] loops firing a given number of bangs (left outlet) and outputs a count for each bang (right outlet). The middle outlet bangs after the loop is done. The 1st argument is the number of bangs. The counter starts from a given offset (2nd argument).

title: vectral~

messages.description: output index of the processed vector/block
input index of the vector/block being processed

methods.description: linear ramp mode, values are <up, down> time
logarithmic ramp mode, values are <up, down> time
change limited mode, values are <up, down> limit
sets the last frame values to "0

cyclone/vectral~.body: [vectral~] is useful for smoothening/filtering frame based signal data such as the output of [fft~], mostly for viewing purposes.

title: wave~

messages.description: phase signal to read the array
the specified portion of the given wavetable channel

arguments.default: length of the array in ms

cyclone/wave~.body: With a phase signal input (from 0 and 1), [wave~] reads a given table. It has many interpolation options and can set a start and end point in the array.

title: xbendin
cyclone/xbendin.body: [xbendin] retrieves 14-bit pitch bend messages from raw MIDI input data.

title: xbendin2
cyclone/xbendin2.body: [xbendin2] retrieves the Most and Least Significant Byte (7-bits values) from pitch bend messages of incoming raw MIDI data. Both can be combined to generate a 14-bit value.

title: xbendout
cyclone/xbendout.body: [xbendout] formats and sends messages that occupy both bytes of the MIDI pitch bend message (14 bit from 0 - 16383).

title: xbendout2
cyclone/xbendout2.body: [xbendout2] formats and sends pitch bend messages as two 7-bit messages (values from 0-127), the Most Significant Byte (MSB) and the Least Significant Byte (LSB).

title: xnotein

messages.description: velocity of note on and note off messages

cyclone/xnotein.body: [xnotein] is more powerful than [notein] as it retrieves (from raw MIDI data streams) not only Note On Velocity but also Note Off (Release) velocity.

title: xnoteout

messages.description: velocity of note on and note off messages

cyclone/xnoteout.body: [xnoteout] is more powerful than [noteout] as it send not only Note On Velocity but also Note Off (Release) velocity.

title: zerox~

messages.description: number of zero crossings per signal block
a click (impulse) at every zero crossing

methods.description: set impulse value sent to right outlet

cyclone/zerox~.body:
[zerox~] functions as a zero-crossing detector and/or a zero-crossing counter (for transient detection). 
Left outlet outputs a value that corresponds to the number of zero crossings per signal block - so it depends on the block size. Right outlet send an impulse at every zero crossing.

title: zl.change

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
list to pass on when it differs from the previous one
sets the list to compare the next input with
the input list, when it differs from the previous one
1 for a new list, 0 for a repeated one

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.change.body: [zl.change] filters out repeated lists: the input only goes out the left outlet when it differs from the previous one, and the right outlet sends 1 for a new list and 0 for a repeated one. The arguments set the initial list to compare with.

title: zl.compare

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
1 if the lists are equal, 0 if not
number of indexes that differ, when the lists aren't equal

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.compare.body: [zl.compare] compares the list in its left inlet with the one in its right inlet (or the arguments), and outputs 1 if they're the same and 0 if not. When they differ, the right outlet sends the number of indexes that aren't equal.

title: zl.delace
cyclone/zl.delace.description: de-interleave a list into two lists

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.delace.body: [zl.delace] de-interleaves a list into two lists: the 1st, 3rd, 5th... elements go out the left outlet, and the 2nd, 4th, 6th... ones out the right outlet.

title: zl.ecils
cyclone/zl.ecils.description: slice a list from its end

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.ecils.body: [zl.ecils] slices a list from its end ('ecils' is 'slice' backwards): split at 'n', the left outlet sends the last 'n' elements and the right outlet the elements before them. The argument or the right inlet sets the split point; 0 means no slicing.

title: zl.filter

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
the list without the removed items
indexes of the items that are kept

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.filter.body: [zl.filter] removes items from a list: the items to remove are set by the arguments or the right inlet. The left outlet sends what remains, and the right outlet the indexes of those items.

title: zl.group
cyclone/zl.group.description: group elements into lists of a given size

messages.description: outputs and clears the remaining stored elements

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.group.body: [zl.group] collects incoming elements into lists of 'n' elements, where 'n' can't be larger than the maximum list size. Each time a group is full it goes out the left outlet, and the remaining elements are kept for the next one. A bang outputs and clears what's stored. The argument or the right inlet sets the group size.

title: zl.indexmap
cyclone/zl.indexmap.description: build a list from elements at given indexes

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
list to take the elements from
0-based indexes of the elements to take
the elements at the given indexes

arguments.description: 0-based indexes of the elements to take

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.indexmap.body: [zl.indexmap] builds a new list from the incoming one, taking the elements at the indexes (0-based) set by the arguments or the right inlet. Indexes out of range are clamped to 0.

title: zl.iter
cyclone/zl.iter.description: split a list into lists of a given size

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
size of the lists to output
successive lists of the given size

arguments.description: size of the lists to output, minimum 1

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.iter.body: [zl.iter] breaks a list into successive lists of a given size; a shorter last part is output too. The argument or the right inlet sets the size, which is at least 1; the default 0 does nothing.

title: zl.join

messages.description: resends the last output, or joins again after a new right list
list to join the right list to
list to append to the input

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.join.body: [zl.join] joins the list in its left inlet with the one in its right inlet (or the arguments), keeping duplicates. A bang resends the last output, or joins again if the right inlet got a new list.

title: zl

messages.description: performs the mode's operation on the current data
one or more element messages to be processed

methods.description: sets the mode (change, compare, delace, ecils, group, indexmap, iter, join, lace, len, lookup, median, mth, nth, queue, reg, rev, rot, sect, scramble, slice, sort, stack, stream, sub, sum, swap, thin, union or unique)
clears mode's arguments and received data in both inlets
sets the maximum list size (1 - 32767, default 256)

cyclone/zl.body: [zl] processes messages with one or more elements ("list messages' or "anything") according to a mode (set via argument/message).

title: zl.lace

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.lace.body: [zl.lace] interleaves the list in its left inlet with the one in its right inlet (or the arguments): 'A B C' and '1 2 3' give 'A 1 B 2 C 3'.

title: zl.len
cyclone/zl.len.description: count the elements of a list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.len.body: [zl.len] outputs how many elements a list has. A bang resends the last output.

title: zl.lookup
cyclone/zl.lookup.description: look up elements of a list by index

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
0-based indexes of the elements to output
the elements at the given indexes

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.lookup.body: [zl.lookup] outputs elements of a stored list: the arguments or the right inlet set the list, and the indexes (0-based) in the left inlet choose the elements.

title: zl.median

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.median.body: [zl.median] outputs the median of a list of numbers.

title: zl.mth
cyclone/zl.mth.description: get an element of a list, counting from 0

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
list to take the element from
index, optionally followed by a replacement element
the other elements, with the replacement in its place if one is set

arguments.description: index of the element, counting from 0
replacement for the element in the right outlet's list (optional)

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.mth.body: [zl.mth] outputs the element at an index, counting from 0, through the left outlet, and the remaining elements through the right outlet. If a replacement is set, it takes the element's place in the right outlet's list. An index out of range, or negative, sends all elements to the right outlet. [zl.nth] counts from 1 instead.

title: zl.nth
cyclone/zl.nth.description: get an element of a list, counting from 1

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
list to take the element from
index, optionally followed by a replacement element
the other elements, with the replacement in its place if one is set

arguments.description: index of the element, counting from 1
replacement for the element in the right outlet's list (optional)

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.nth.body: [zl.nth] outputs the element at an index, counting from 1, through the left outlet, and the remaining elements through the right outlet. If a replacement is set, it takes the element's place in the right outlet's list. With an index of 0 (the default) or out of range, all elements go to the right outlet. [zl.mth] counts from 0 instead.

title: zl.queue
cyclone/zl.queue.description: first in, first out element storage

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.queue.body: [zl.queue] stores elements first in, first out: each incoming list adds its elements, and each bang outputs the oldest one. The right outlet sends the number of stored elements.

title: zl.reg

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.reg.body: [zl.reg] stores a list: the left inlet stores and outputs it, the right inlet only stores it, and a bang outputs it. The arguments set the initially stored list.

title: zl.rev

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.rev.body: [zl.rev] reverses the order of the elements of a list. A bang resends the last output.

title: zl.rot

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
rotation, positive to the right, negative to the left

arguments.description: rotation, positive to the right, negative to the left

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.rot.body: [zl.rot] rotates a list: with a positive rotation 'n', the elements shift 'n' positions to the right and the last 'n' wrap around to the start; a negative 'n' rotates the other way. The argument or the right inlet sets the rotation.

title: zl.scramble
cyclone/zl.scramble.description: put the elements of a list in random order

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
sets the list to scramble without output
the original indexes, in their new order

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.scramble.body: [zl.scramble] puts the elements of a list in random order. The right outlet sends the original indexes of the elements in their new order.

title: zl.sect
cyclone/zl.sect.description: elements two lists have in common

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
the elements that are also in the other list
when there are no common elements

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.sect.body: [zl.sect] outputs the elements of the input list that are also in another list, set by the arguments or the right inlet. When there are none, the right outlet sends a bang.

title: zl.slice

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.slice.body: [zl.slice] slices a list: split at 'n', the left outlet sends the first 'n' elements and the right outlet the remaining ones. The argument or the right inlet sets the split point; 0 means no slicing.

title: zl.sort

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
the original indexes, in sorted order

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.sort.body: [zl.sort] sorts the elements of a list, in ascending order by default or descending with -1. The right outlet sends the original indexes of the elements in their sorted order.

title: zl.stack
cyclone/zl.stack.description: last in, first out element storage

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.stack.body: [zl.stack] stores elements last in, first out: each incoming list adds its elements, and each bang outputs the most recent one. The right outlet sends the number of stored elements.

title: zl.stream
cyclone/zl.stream.description: list of the last N elements received

messages.description: 1 once N elements were received, 0 before that

arguments.description: number of elements N, negative reverses the list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.stream.body: [zl.stream] outputs a list of the last N elements it received; a negative N reverses the list. The right outlet sends 1 once N elements were received and 0 before that. A bang resends the last output.

title: zl.sub
cyclone/zl.sub.description: find a sublist in a list

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
position of each occurrence, counting from 1

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.sub.body: [zl.sub] searches a list for occurrences of another one, set by the arguments or the right inlet. The right outlet sends the number of occurrences, and the left outlet the position of each one, counting from 1. When there are none, the right outlet sends 0.

title: zl.sum

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.sum.body: [zl.sum] outputs the sum of the numbers in a list; symbols are ignored.

title: zl.swap

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
the list with the elements swapped

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.swap.body: [zl.swap] swaps elements of a list: the arguments or the right inlet give pairs of indexes (0-based) whose elements trade places.

title: zl.thin

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.thin.body: [zl.thin] removes all duplicates from a list.

title: zl.union

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
the first list, followed by the elements of the second it doesn't have

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.union.body: [zl.union] joins two lists without duplicating the elements of the second list that are already in the first. The arguments set the initial second list.

title: zl.unique
cyclone/zl.unique.description: remove given items from a list

messages.description: performs the operation again on the last received list
the list without the removed items

methods.description: clears the mode's arguments and the data received in both inlets
sets the maximum list size, 1 to 32767

cyclone/zl.unique.body: [zl.unique] removes items from a list: the items to remove are set by the arguments or the right inlet. Unlike [zl.filter], it doesn't output the indexes of the remaining items.

title: hv.comb~
heavylib/hv.comb~.body: [hv.comb~] is a comb filter. Its right inlet takes messages that set the feedforward and feedback amounts, the input and output delay times, and the interpolation time for delay changes.

title: hv.compressor2~
heavylib/hv.compressor2~.body: stereo compressor, static 40ms attack/release, adjustable threshold and ratio settings

title: hv.compressor~
heavylib/hv.compressor~.body: mono compressor, static 40ms attack/release, adjustable threshold and ratio settings

title: hv.dispatch
heavylib/hv.dispatch.description: automatically generate local send object for parameter distribution

messages.description: parameter name followed by message to send
input with matching parameter and message trimmed

heavylib/hv.dispatch.body: hv.dispatch creates local send objects. it's a way to funnel messages into a single abstraction input and then easily be able to distribute them. it outputs the remainder of messages, so that you can chain them together.

title: hv.drunk

messages.description: generate and output next random number

heavylib/hv.drunk.body: A random walk (drunk) is a special case of a Markov chain, in which the states are integers and the transitions add or subtract a small amount (or zero) from the previous state to get a new one. Here the "f" holds the state. When it gets a bang, the previous state is added to a random number (from 0 to $bound) multiplied by a random sign (-1 or 1). The new value is then coerced into the range from 0 to $bound

title: hv.envfollow~
heavylib/hv.envfollow~.description: envelope follower with adjustable attack parameter
heavylib/hv.envfollow~.body: [hv.envfollow~] is an envelope follower with adjustable attack and release times.

title: hv.eq~
heavylib/hv.eq~.body: [hv.eq~] outputs a signal that is 1 where its left input is equal to its right input, and 0 elsewhere.

title: hv.exp~
heavylib/hv.exp~.description: alternative implementation to the exp~ object
heavylib/hv.exp~.body: This abstraction presents an alternative implementation to the exp~ object. Heavy uses the system's expf() function (as does Pd), but some applications may wish to avoid the expf() function entirely, and instead use this reasonably fast approximation.

title: hv.filter.gain~
heavylib/hv.filter.gain~.description: generic filter module with swappable filter types and frequency, Q and gain settings
heavylib/hv.filter.gain~.body: [hv.filter.gain~] is a filter with a selectable type (highshelf, lowshelf or peak) and frequency, Q and gain settings. It updates its coefficients at signal rate, to avoid clicks when sweeping the controls.

title: hv.filter~
heavylib/hv.filter~.description: generic filter module with swappable filter types and frequency, Q settings

arguments.description: filter type <allpass, lowpass, highpass, bandpass1, bandpass2, or notch>

heavylib/hv.filter~.body: [hv.filter~] is a filter with a selectable type (allpass, lowpass, highpass, bandpass1, bandpass2 or notch) and frequency and Q settings. It updates its coefficients at signal rate, to avoid clicks when sweeping the controls.

title: hv.flanger2~
heavylib/hv.flanger2~.body: [hv.flanger2~] is a stereo flanger. Its right inlet takes messages that set the dry/wet mix, feedback, speed and intensity, and the argument sets the delay time.

title: hv.flanger~
heavylib/hv.flanger~.body: [hv.flanger~] is a mono flanger. Its right inlet takes messages that set the dry/wet mix, feedback, speed and intensity, and the argument sets the delay time.

title: hv.freqshift~
heavylib/hv.freqshift~.body: [hv.freqshift~] is a frequency shifter: it shifts all frequencies of its input by the amount in Hz set in the right inlet.

title: hv.gte~

messages.description: 1 if left input >= right input, 0 otherwise

heavylib/hv.gte~.body: [hv.gte~] outputs a signal that is 1 where its left input is greater than or equal to its right input, and 0 elsewhere.

title: hv.gt~

messages.description: 1 if left is greater than right input, 0 otherwise

heavylib/hv.gt~.body: [hv.gt~] outputs a signal that is 1 where its left input is greater than its right input, and 0 elsewhere.

title: hv.hip~
heavylib/hv.hip~.description: highpass variant of [rpole~] with signal-controlled cutoff
heavylib/hv.hip~.body: [hv.hip~] is a variant of [hip~] with a signal-controlled cutoff frequency. Like [hip~], it has no effect when the cutoff is above the sample rate divided by 2 pi.

title: hv.lfo
heavylib/hv.lfo.description: precision LFOs based on sampled signal oscillators

arguments.description: wave shape, <sine, ramp, saw, square or pulse>

heavylib/hv.lfo.body: [hv.lfo] is a precise control rate LFO based on sampled signal oscillators, with sine, ramp, saw, square or pulse shapes. It outputs values between 0 and 1; the right inlet resets the phase, or sets the pulse width for the pulse shape.

title: hv.log~
heavylib/hv.log~.body: Signal rate logarithm operation. The left inlet must be a signal and the right inlet takes the base. The base may optionally also be initialised with the object. If no base is supplied, then the natural logarithm is assumed (base e).

title: hv.lop~
heavylib/hv.lop~.description: lowpass variant of [rpole~] with signal-controlled cutoff
heavylib/hv.lop~.body: [hv.lop~] is a variant of [lop~] with a signal-controlled cutoff frequency. Like [lop~], it has no effect when the cutoff is above the sample rate divided by 2 pi.

title: hv.lte~

messages.description: 1 if left input is <= right input, 0 otherwise

heavylib/hv.lte~.body: [hv.lte~] outputs a signal that is 1 where its left input is less than or equal to its right input, and 0 elsewhere.

title: hv.lt~

messages.description: 1 if left input is less than right input, 0 otherwise

heavylib/hv.lt~.body: [hv.lt~] outputs a signal that is 1 where its left input is less than its right input, and 0 elsewhere.

title: hv.multiplex~

messages.description: signal a if lhs > rhs, signal b otherwise

heavylib/hv.multiplex~.body: [hv.multiplex~] outputs one of two input signals depending on a comparison: signal a where the left-hand side is greater than the right-hand side, and signal b otherwise.

title: hv.neq~

vanilla/bag.body:
The bag object adds a value to or removes it from a collection of numbers depending on the flag. The left inlet takes the value and the right inlet takes the flag. If the flag is true (nonzero), the value is added to the collection and removed otherwise. The example here takes a list input, which gets spread at inlets (as is common in Pd).

The collection may have many copies of the same value. You can output the collection (and empty it) with a "flush" message, or just empty it with "clear." You can use this to mimic a sustain pedal, for example.

messages.description: at every DSP block cycle when DSP is on

vanilla/bang~.body:
bang~ outputs a bang after each DSP block cycle (at the same logical time as the DSP cycle.) This is primarily useful for sampling the outputs of analysis algorithms.

By default, a block size is 64 samples, at a 44100 sample rate, this about 1.45 ms. You can change the sample rate in audio settings and the block size with the block~ or switch~ object. Note that the minimum block size bang~ can handle is 64!

title: bendin
vanilla/bendin.body: [bendin] outputs pitch bend values from MIDI input, with their channel. Known bug: [bendin] and [bendout] are inconsistent: [bendin] outputs values from 0 to 16383 and [bendout] takes values from -8192 to 8191. This won't change.

title: bendout
vanilla/bendout.body: [bendout] sends pitch bend values to MIDI output, on the given channel. Known bug: [bendin] and [bendout] are inconsistent: [bendin] outputs values from 0 to 16383 and [bendout] takes values from -8192 to 8191. This won't change.

vanilla/biquad~.body:
Biquad~ calculates the following difference equation:
y(n) = ff1 * w(n) + ff2 * w(n-1) + ff3 * w(n-2)
w(n) = x(n) + fb1 * w(n-1) + fb2 * w(n-2)

The filter's coefficients syntax (set via arguments or list input) is: fb1 fb2 ff1 ff2 ff3

title: bob~
vanilla/bob~.description: Runge-Kutte numerical simulation of the Moog analog resonant filter

messages.description: resonant or cutoff frequency in Hz

methods.description: post internal state and parameters on Pd's window

vanilla/bob~.body:
The design of bob~ is based on papers by Tim Stilson, Timothy E. Stinchcombe, and Antti Huovilainen. See README.txt for pointers. The three audio inputs are the signal to filter, the cutoff/resonant frequency in cycles per second, and "resonance" (the sharpness of the filter). Nominally, a resonance of 4 should be the limit of stability -- above that, the filter oscillates.

By default bob~ does one step of 4th-order Runge-Kutte integration per audio sample. This works OK for resonant/cutoff frequencies up to about 1/2 Nyquist. To improve accuracy and/or to extend the range of the filter to higher cutoff frequencies you can oversample by any factor - but note that computation time rises accordingly. At high cutoff frequencies/resonance values the RK approximation can go unstable. You can combat this by raising the oversampling factor.

The saturation parameter determines at what signal level the "transistors" in the model saturate. The maximum output amplitude is about 2/3 of that value. "Clear" momentarily shorts out the capacitors in case the filter has gone unstable and stopped working.

Compatibility note: there was a bug in this module, fixed for Pd version 0.52. You can get the (incorrect) pre-0.52 behavior by setting pd's compatibility level to 0.51.

vanilla/bonk~.body: [bonk~] detects attacks in an audio signal and measures its spectral envelope. It reports each attack with its loudness in 11 frequency bands, and can learn templates to tell different instruments apart.

title: bp~
vanilla/bp~.body: [bp~] is a 2-pole bandpass filter: it passes a sinusoid at the center frequency at about unit gain and attenuates other frequencies. The middle inlet sets the center frequency and the right one the Q; the higher the Q, the narrower the band. The center frequency can be at most the sample rate divided by 6.28; for a more general filter, try [vcf~].

title: catch~
vanilla/catch~.description: catch signal from one or more throw~ objects
vanilla/catch~.body:
Any number of throw~ objects can add into one catch~ object (but two catch~ objects cannot share the same name).

Note: the [throw~] objects have to be sorted before the [catch~] in the DSP chain, or else you'll never get less than a block's delay.

title: change
vanilla/change.description: remove repeated numbers from a stream
vanilla/change.body: [change] outputs its input only when it differs from the previous value, filtering out repetitions. 'set' changes the current value without output, and a bang outputs it.

title: choice
vanilla/choice.description: search for a best match to an incoming list

messages.description: outputs the index of the stored vector that matches best

methods.description: post debugging information in the print out window

vanilla/choice.body:
The choice object holds a list of vectors, each having up to ten elements. When sent a list of numbers, it outputs the index of the known vector that matches most closely. The quality of the match is the dot product of the two vectors after normalizing them, i.e., the vector whose direction is closest to that of the input wins.

If given a nonzero creation argument, choice tries to avoid repetitious outputs by weighting less recently output vectors preferentially.

You can use this to choose interactively between a number of behaviors depending on their attributes. For example, you might have stored a number of melodies, of which some are syncopated, some chromatic, some are more than 100 years old, some are bugle calls, and some are Christmas carols. You could then ask to find a syncopated bugle call (1, 0, 0, 1, 0) and you'll get the thing most closely matching the request.

You can use numbers other than 0 and 1 to indicate relative strengths of the attributes, or even use negative numbers to indicate opposites, either in the incoming lists or in the stored ones.

vanilla/clone.body:
clone creates any number of instances of a desired abstraction (a patch loaded as an object in another patch). Within each copy, "$1" is set to the instance number. These count from 0 unless the "-s" option sets another start, and the "-x" option leaves "$1" out. You can pass additional arguments to the copies, which appear as $2 and onward (or $1 and onward with the "-x" option).

clone's inlets and outlets correspond to those of the contained patch, and may be signal and/or control inlets and outlets. You can click on the clone object to see the first of the created instances.

Control inlets forward a message to the instance whose number starts it, or use the 'next', 'this', 'set' and 'all' prefixes to pick instances. Signal inlets can get non float messages with the 'fwd' prefix in the same way, but signals are sent to all the instances. Signal outlets output the sum of all instances' outputs, and control outlets forward messages with the number of the instance prepended to them.

For backward compatibility, you can also invoke this as "clone 16 clone-abstraction", swapping the abstraction name and the number of voices.

title: complex-mod~
vanilla/complex-mod~.body:
The complex modulator takes two signals in which it considers to be the real and imaginary part of a complex-valued signal. It then does a complex multiplication by a sinusoid to shift all frequencies up or down by any frequency shift in Hz.

This is also known as 'single side band modulation' and relates to ring modulation (which has two sidebands)

The left output is the frequency shifted by the amount of the frequency shift. The right outlet gives us the other side band, which is shifted by the same amount in reverse.

(for instance, if the shift is 100, left output shifts the frequency up by 100 and the right shifts it down by 100)

title: cos
vanilla/cos.body: [cos] outputs the cosine of its input, an angle in radians. Unlike the signal object [cos~], which takes its input in cycles (0 to 1), the control-rate trigonometric functions use radians.

title: cos~

messages.description: input from 0-1 (wraps into 0-1 if outside this range)
phase ramp (in the range of 0 to 1)

vanilla/cos~.body: The cos~ object outputs the cosine of two pi times its signal input. So -1, 0, 1 and 2 give 1 out, 0.5 gives -1, and so on.

title: cpole~

arguments.description: real and imaginary part of coefficient

methods.description: set internal state (real and imaginary part)
clear internal state to zero (same as "set 0 0")

vanilla/cpole~.body:
cpole~ filters a complex audio signal (first two inlets) via a raw one-pole (recursive) filter, whose coefficients are controlled by creation arguments or by another complex audio signal (remaining two inlets).

The action of cpole~ is:
y[n] = x[n] + a[n] * y[n-1]
where y[n] is the output, x[n] the input, and a[n] the filter coefficient (all complex numbers). The filter is unstable if/when |a[n]| > 1.

The transfer function is H(Z) = 1/(1 - aZ^-1).

Pd also provides a suite of user-friendly filters. This and other raw filters are provided for situations which the user-friendly ones can't handle. See Chapter 8 of http://msp.ucsd.edu/techniques/latest/book-html/node127.html for an introduction to the necessary theory.

title: cputime
vanilla/cputime.body: The cputime object measures elapsed CPU time,  as measured by your operating system. This appears to work on NT,  IRIX,  and Linux,  but not on W98.

title: ctlin
vanilla/ctlin.body: [ctlin] outputs MIDI control change messages: the value, controller number and channel. The first argument sets a controller number and the second a channel, each removing the matching outlet. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: ctlout
vanilla/ctlout.body: [ctlout] sends MIDI control change messages: a value, on the controller number and channel set by the arguments or the right inlets (channel 1 by default). Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: czero_rev~

arguments.description: real and imaginary part of coefficient

methods.description: set internal state (real and imaginary part)
clear internal state to zero (same as "set 0 0")

vanilla/czero_rev~.body:
Czero_rev~ filters a complex audio signal (first two inlets) via a raw one-zero (non-recursive) filter, whose coefficients are controlled by creation arguments or by another complex audio signal (remaining two inlets). The impulse response is that of [czero~] reversed in time.

The action of czero_rev~ is:
y[n] = - a[n] * x[n] + x[n-1]
where y[n] is the output, x[n] the input, and a[n] the filter coefficient (all complex numbers). The filter is always stable.

The transfer function is H(Z) = -a + Z^-1.

Pd also provides a suite of user-friendly filters. This and other raw filters are provided for situations which the user-friendly ones can't handle. See Chapter 8 of http://msp.ucsd.edu/techniques/latest/book-html/node127.html for an introduction to the necessary theory.

title: czero~

arguments.description: real and imaginary part of coefficient

methods.description: set internal state (real and imaginary part)
clear internal state to zero (same as "set 0 0")

vanilla/czero~.body:
czero~ filters a complex audio signal (first two inlets) via a raw one-zero (non-recursive) filter, whose coefficients are controlled by creation arguments or by another complex audio signal (remaining two inlets).

The action of czero~ is:
y[n] = x[n] - a[n] * x[n-1]
where y[n] is the output, x[n] the input, and a[n] the filter coefficient (all complex numbers). The filter is always stable.

The transfer function is H(Z) = 1 - aZ^-1.

Pd also provides a suite of user-friendly filters. This and other raw filters are provided for situations which the user-friendly ones can't handle. See Chapter 8 of http://msp.ucsd.edu/techniques/latest/book-html/node127.html for an introduction to the necessary theory.

title: dac~
vanilla/dac~.body:
adc~ and dac~ provide real-time audio input and output for Pd, respectively, whether analog or digital. By default they are stereo (with channel numbers 1, 2), but you can specify different channel numbers via arguments.

The actual number of channels Pd inputs and outputs is set in the audio settings. You can open patches that want to use more channels, and channel numbers out of range will be dropped in dac~ or output zero in adc~.

If more than one dac~ outputs to the same channel, the signals are added. More than one adc~ can output the same input channel.

title: dbtopow
vanilla/dbtopow.body: [dbtopow] converts dB to power units, equal to the square of the "RMS" amplitude, so that 100 dB corresponds to a power of 1. Zero dB and less output zero. [powtodb] does the reverse.

title: dbtopow~

title: declare

flags.name: -path <symbol>
flags.description: add to search path, relative to the patch or user paths

flags.name: -stdpath <symbol>

flags.name: -lib <symbol>
flags.description: load a library, relative to the patch or user paths

flags.name: -stdlib <symbol>
flags.description: load a library, relative to Pd (the 'extra' folder)

vanilla/declare.body:
Compiled external libraries come either as a single binary pack (the "classic" library format) or as a set of separate binaries and/or abstractions. A single binary pack is what we refer to as a 'library' and needs to be pre loaded - whereas external libraries that have separate binaries/abstractions can be loaded by simply adding its directory to the search path. Adding a directory to the path is also needed if you want to load things like audio and text files that are in it.

A declare object adds one or more directories to the search path and/or pre-loads one or more libraries ("externals") to Pd in preparation for opening the patch from a file. The usage is "declare [-flag value] [-flag value] ..." (For any of these you may use a full pathname such as "/tmp/dir" or, in Windows, "C:/garbage" instead of a relative path).

For instance, if you put abstractions and/or other supporting files in a subdirectory "more", you can put an object "declare -path more" to make sure Pd sees them when the patch is loaded. Or, if you have files installed in the directory extra/stillmore (in the Pd installation) you can get it using "declare -stdpath stillmore".

Paths declared with '-path' will have top search priority. Next priority is the relative path, then user added search paths (set in "Preferences => Path") and finally the standard path (a.k.a the 'extra' folder). As of version 0.49, "declare -path" and "declare -lib" will fall back the other search paths if the relative path to the patch does not exist. To avoid checking further, use an explicit relative path by prepending "./" or "../" to the path or lib name.

Since the 'extra' folder is the last in the search priority, other paths are searched before. You can use [declare -stdpath ./] to ensure that 'extra' has search priority. Note that the order you specify '-path' flags also specify the search priority.

It is a current best practice to just use [declare] instead of permanently adding paths to the user search paths or libs to startup. With [declare] you can better manage and avoid conflicts with externals from different libraries that have the same name by using it to call the right library you want.

However, note that when you load a library (with 'declare -lib' or via startup), all of its objects get pre loaded and prevail, so using 'declare -path' cannot enforce loading priority. Hence, you may need to adopt slash declarations as in [library/objectname]. Also Note that while '-path' will only add search paths for the patch that owns the [declare] object, once a library is loaded, it stays with Pd and will be able to be loaded in other patches without [declare]. For more details on this and how external loading works in Pd, please refer to the chapter 4 of Pd's manual.

WARNING: as of version 0.47, "declare -path" and "declare -stdpath" inside abstractions take effect only within those abstractions. If Pd's compatibility version is set to 0.46 or earlier the old (buggy) behavior takes effect.

BUG: The name "-stdpath" is confusing, as it has a quite different effect from "-stdpath" on the pd command line.

vanilla/delay.body: [delay] outputs a bang after a delay time, set by the argument or the right inlet. title: delread4~

vanilla/delread4~.description: read a delay line with 4-point interpolation
vanilla/delread4~.body:
[delread4~] implements a 4-point interpolating delay tap. The delay time in ms is set by an incoming signal, so it can vary continuously.

[delread~] and [delread4~] read from a delay line allocated in a [delwrite~] object with the same name. More than one of them can read from the same [delwrite~]. If the delay time is longer than the delay line or less than zero, it is clipped to the length of the delay line. Delay names often use "$0" (the patch ID number) to keep them local to a patch.

In case the [delwrite~] runs later in the DSP loop than the [delread~] or [delread4~] objects, the delay is constrained below by one vector length (usually 64 samples).

title: delread~
vanilla/delread~.body:
delread~ and delread4~ objects read from a delay line allocated in a delwrite~ object with the same name. You can use more than one delread~ and/or delread4~ object for the same delwrite~. If the specified delay time is longer than the delay line or less than zero, it is clipped to the length of the delay line. Delay names often use "$0" (the patch ID number) to keep them local to a patch.

In case the delwrite~ runs later in the DSP loop than the delread~ or delread4~ objects, the delay is constrained below by one vector length (usually 64 samples).

vanilla/delwrite~.body:
[delwrite~] allocates a delay line with the given name and size in ms, and writes its signal input into it.

[delread~] and [delread4~] read from a delay line allocated in a [delwrite~] object with the same name. More than one of them can read from the same [delwrite~]. If the delay time is longer than the delay line or less than zero, it is clipped to the length of the delay line. Delay names often use "$0" (the patch ID number) to keep them local to a patch.

In case the [delwrite~] runs later in the DSP loop than the [delread~] or [delread4~] objects, the delay is constrained below by one vector length (usually 64 samples).

vanilla/element.body:
"element" takes a pointer at right and an index number at left. It looks up a field from the pointer, which should be an array, and outputs the element of the array specified by the index number. title: expr

arguments.description: expression including operators, functions, inlet types, float and symbols

vanilla/expr.body:
[expr] evaluates C-like expressions at control rate. Inlets are defined by variables of the form $t#, where 't' is the type and # is the inlet number, counting from 1 at the left (up to 100): $f# is a float, $i# is an integer (floats are truncated) and $s# is a symbol, used for array names. Text in quotes is a symbol string, and [expr] can also output symbols.

Multiple expressions separated by semicolons (up to 100) create one outlet each. They are evaluated from right to left, so the rightmost outlet fires first.

Arrays and variables (defined with [value]) are accessed as in C: "tab[5]" is element 5 of the array "tab", "$s2[5]" is element 5 of the array whose name came into inlet 2, and "valx + 10" adds 10 to the [value] named "valx". The store function "=" writes the result of an operation into a variable or array index, as in "tab[$f1] = $f2".

Besides the C operators (arithmetic, relational, bitwise and logical), the available functions are:
math: min, max, int, rint, round, trunc, nearbyint, float, abs, fmod, remainder, floor, ceil, modf, imodf, copysign, ldexp, hypot, if, random, isnan, isinf, finite
power and log: pow, sqrt, cbrt, exp, expm1, ln, log, log10, log1p, fact, erf, erfc
trigonometry: sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2, sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh
tables: size, sum, Sum, avg, Avg
acoustics: mtof, ftom, dbtorms, rmstodb, dbtopow, powtodb
symbols and strings: symbol, sym, var, strlen, strcat, strncat, strcmp, strncmp, strcasecmp, strncasecmp, strpbrk, strspn, strcspn, tolower, tonlower, toupper, tonupper

result of an expression, one outlet per expression

arguments.description: expression including operators, functions, inlet types, float and symbols

vanilla/expr~.body:
[expr~] evaluates C-like expressions on signals, vector by vector, combining signal and control processing. It works like [expr] with the addition of $v# for signal inputs, which is needed at least for the first inlet: "$v1" makes the first inlet a signal input. Inlets are defined by variables of the form $t#, where 't' is the type and # is the inlet number, counting from 1 at the left (up to 100): $f# is a float, $i# is an integer (floats are truncated) and $s# is a symbol, used for array names. Signal and control inlets can be mixed in any order.

The result is a signal. Multiple expressions separated by semicolons (up to 100) create one outlet each.

Arrays and variables (defined with [value]) are accessed as in C: "tab[5]" is element 5 of the array "tab", "$s2[5]" is element 5 of the array whose name came into inlet 2, and "valx + 10" adds 10 to the [value] named "valx". The store function "=" writes the result of an operation into a variable or array index, as in "tab[$f1] = $f2".

Besides the C operators (arithmetic, relational, bitwise and logical), the available functions are:
math: min, max, int, rint, round, trunc, nearbyint, float, abs, fmod, remainder, floor, ceil, modf, imodf, copysign, ldexp, hypot, if, random, isnan, isinf, finite
power and log: pow, sqrt, cbrt, exp, expm1, ln, log, log10, log1p, fact, erf, erfc
trigonometry: sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2, sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh
tables: size, sum, Sum, avg, Avg
acoustics: mtof, ftom, dbtorms, rmstodb, dbtopow, powtodb
Functions that output a symbol only work in [expr].

title: fexpr~

arguments.description: expression including operators, functions, inlet types, float and symbols

methods.description: set values for previous input/output values
clear input/output memory, optional symbol specifies a specific input (such as x1) or output (y1)

vanilla/fexpr~.body:
[fexpr~] evaluates expressions sample by sample with access to previous input and output samples, which makes it a flexible tool for building FIR and IIR filters. It works like [expr] with the addition of $x# for signal inputs and $y# for previous outputs. Inlets are defined by variables of the form $t#, where 't' is the type and # is the inlet number, counting from 1 at the left (up to 100): $f# is a float, $i# is an integer (floats are truncated) and $s# is a symbol, used for array names.

$x# is followed by a sample index in brackets: "$x1[-1]" is the previous sample of the first inlet, and without brackets the current sample is implied, so a filter that averages each sample with the previous one is "fexpr~ ($x1 + $x1[-1])/2". $y# accesses previous output samples of expression #, indexed from -1. Indexes reach back up to the block size (64 by default), and fractional indexes are linearly interpolated.

Multiple expressions separated by semicolons (up to 100) create one outlet each.

Arrays and variables (defined with [value]) are accessed as in C: "tab[5]" is element 5 of the array "tab", "$s2[5]" is element 5 of the array whose name came into inlet 2, and "valx + 10" adds 10 to the [value] named "valx". The store function "=" writes the result of an operation into a variable or array index, as in "tab[$f1] = $f2".

Besides the C operators (arithmetic, relational, bitwise and logical), the available functions are:
math: min, max, int, rint, round, trunc, nearbyint, float, abs, fmod, remainder, floor, ceil, modf, imodf, copysign, ldexp, hypot, if, random, isnan, isinf, finite
power and log: pow, sqrt, cbrt, exp, expm1, ln, log, log10, log1p, fact, erf, erfc
trigonometry: sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2, sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh

vanilla/fft~.body:
[fft~] does a forward complex Fourier analysis: its inlets take the real and imaginary parts of a signal, and its outlets give those of the spectrum.

The analysis size is one block, which you can set with [block~] or [switch~]. There is no normalization, so an FFT followed by an IFFT has a gain of N.

vanilla/file-glob.body:
cross-platform notes on globbing:

[file glob] attempts to unify the behaviour of wildcard matching on different platforms. as such, it does not support all features of a given pattern matching implementation (or only accidentally).

the following rules should help you to write patches that use platform independent globbing.

- the pattern may contain the wildcards '*' (for any number of characters) and '?' (for a single character) in the last path component. no other wildcards are supported.

- the behaviour of patterns that contain wildcards in a path component other than the last one is *undefined* (and platform dependent). DO NOT USE THIS.

- patterns ending with '/' will ONLY match directories

- patterns ending with anything else will match files AND directories

- files/dirs starting with a "." only match if the matching pattern explicitly contains the leading dot.

- the special files/dirs "." and ".." only match if requested explicitly, never with a wildcard pattern.

'splitext' separates the directory+file component from the extension of the given path, and outputs a list with both on the 1st outlet.

If no extension is found, the path is sent to the 2nd outlet.

An extension is a non-empty string after the last '.' in the filename-component of the path.

NOTE: the 'file split*' objects will always output (lists of) symbols, even if the component looks like a number. on one hand this makes it harder to [route], but on the other hand this will keep zero-padded numbers intact (think "2020/01/01/0042.wav").

No checks are made on whether the path is valid or exists. It always outputs symbols, even if a component looks like a number: that makes them harder to [route], but keeps zero-padded numbers intact (think "2020/01/01/0042.wav").
