symbols that look like a float are converted, stored and output

methods.description: send the stored value to a [receive] or [value] object that has the same name as the symbol (no output)

vanilla/float.body: [float] stores a number. A float in the left inlet stores and outputs it, a float in the right inlet stores it without output, and a bang outputs the stored number.

title: floatbox
vanilla/floatbox.body: [floatbox] is a number box: it shows and outputs a number. Click and drag to change it (shift-drag for hundredths), or click it, type a value and hit enter. 'set' changes the value without output, and a bang outputs it.

title: framp~
vanilla/framp~.description: estimate frequency and amplitude of FFT
vanilla/framp~.body:
Framp~ takes as input a rectangular-windowed FFT and outputs, for each FFT channel, the estimated amplitude and frequency of any component feeding that channel. A sinusoidal component should appear in four components (or three in the special case of a sinusoid exactly tuned to a bin.) Frequency output is in bins, i.e., units of SR/N.

The estimation is done according to the hop-1 trick described in Puckette&Brown, Accuracy of Frequency Estimates Using the Phase Vocoder, using a Hann window. A more sophisticated version of this technique is used in the sigmund~ object.

title: ftom
vanilla/ftom.body: Takes a frequency value as input and outputs the corresponding MIDI value at A=440

title: ftom~
vanilla/ftom~.description: frequency to MIDI conversion for signals
vanilla/ftom~.body: Takes a frequency signal as input and outputs the corresponding MIDI signal at A=440

title: fudiformat
vanilla/fudiformat.description: FUDI messages to and from Pd lists

messages.description: any message to convert to a FUDI packet

vanilla/fudiformat.body: FUDI stands for "Fast Universal Digital Interface" and is a networking protocol used by Pd. The fudiformat object makes FUDI messages suitable for sending over the network via netsend (in UDP mode). Incoming messages are output as FUDI messages, byte by byte. The '-u' creation argument switches to "UDP" mode, omitting the packet separator. This saves some two bytes, but only works when sending single FUDI messages over UDP. It doesn't work with TCP/IP (however, you can use the default format even with UDP transport).

title: fudiparse
vanilla/fudiparse.description: FUDI messages to and from Pd lists

messages.description: FUDI packet to convert to Pd messages

vanilla/fudiparse.body: The fudiparse object takes incoming lists of numbers, interpreting them as the bytes in a FUDI message (as received when sending Pd-messages via [netreceive -b]).

title: garray
vanilla/garray.description: graphical array (messages received via array name)
vanilla/garray.body: [garray] is the graphical array you put in a patch from the Put menu: a named array of numbers shown in a graph. Messages to its name resize, read, write or fill it.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/ge.body: [>=] outputs 1 if its left input is greater than or equal to its right input, and 0 otherwise.

title: get

messages.description: pointer to a data structure scalar

arguments.description: one or more field names (defines number of outlets)

methods.description: set template and field name (if none or just one argument is given)

vanilla/get.body:
"Get", when sent a pointer to a scalar, retrieves fields from it by name. The fields can be floats or symbols.

If you have data whose template is variable (from a heterogeneous list, for example) you can use the template "-" as a wild card. In Pd 0.47 and earlier, there is no penalty for this, but future versions may run faster with pre-specified templates than with "-" (by looking up the variable names in advance).

title: getsize
vanilla/getsize.description: get size of a data structures array

messages.description: pointer to a scalar with an array field

vanilla/getsize.body:
When sent a pointer of a scalar, "getsize" looks up a field, which should be an array, and outputs the number of elements of the array. The template and field name are specified as creation arguments. The smallest possible size is one.

If you don't know the template name you may specify "-", in which case the object will figure out the template name itself, at some possible cost in efficiency and clarity.

title: graph
vanilla/graph.description: subpatch that you can see inside of
vanilla/graph.body: [graph] is a subpatch with 'graph on parent' enabled: a rectangular region of its contents shows on the parent patch, displaying GUIs, comments, arrays or data structure scalars. Arrays put from the Put menu live in a graph.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/gt.body: [>] outputs 1 if its left input is greater than its right input, and 0 otherwise.

title: hilbert~
vanilla/hilbert~.body: The Hilbert transform (the name is abused here according to computer music tradition) puts out a phase quadrature version of the input signal suitable for signal sideband modulation via complex-mod~.

title: hip~
vanilla/hip~.body: hip~ is a one-pole highpass filter with a specified cutoff frequency. Left (audio) inlet is the incoming audio signal. Right (control) inlet sets cutoff frequency.

title: hradio
hdl
radiobutton
radiobut
rdb

methods.description: nonzero sets to vertical, zero sets to horizontal
sets font type <0: DejaVu Sans Mono, 1: Helvetica, 2: Times> and font size
first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)
sets position in the patch canvas
changes the position by a x/y delta in pixels

vanilla/hradio.body: [hradio] is a horizontal radio button GUI: clicking one of its cells outputs that cell's number. Incoming floats set the value and are passed through, 'set' sets it without output, and a bang outputs it. Right click for properties such as the number of cells, size and colors.

title: hslider
hsl

methods.description: nonzero sets to vertical, zero sets to horizontal
sets font type <0: DejaVu Sans Mono, 1: Helvetica, 2: Times> and font size
first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)
sets position in the patch canvas
changes the position by a x/y delta in pixels
nonzero sets to steady, zero sets to jump on click

vanilla/hslider.body: [hslider] is a horizontal slider GUI: click and drag to output values within its range, or shift-drag for fine tuning. Incoming floats set the value and are passed through, 'set' sets it without output, and a bang outputs it. Its scale can be linear or logarithmic.

title: ifft~

messages.description: real part of signal to transform
imaginary part of signal to transform

vanilla/ifft~.body:
[ifft~] does an inverse complex Fourier transform, turning the real and imaginary parts of a spectrum back into a complex signal.

The analysis size is one block, which you can set with [block~] or [switch~]. There is no normalization, so an FFT followed by an IFFT has a gain of N.

title: inlet
vanilla/inlet.body: [inlet] creates an inlet on the box of the subpatch or abstraction it is in, and outputs the messages that come into it. Inlets are ordered from left to right by their position.

title: inlet~

messages.description: set default value for no signal connected
any other message may be forwarded to right outlet
any message from parent patch or inlet

arguments.description: set upsampling method. 'hold' for sample/hold, 'pad' for zero-padded, and 'lin' for linear interpolation

vanilla/inlet~.body: [inlet~] creates a signal inlet on the box of the subpatch or abstraction it is in, and outputs the signal that comes into it. Other messages to that inlet come out its right outlet, and a float sets the value used when no signal is connected. In a subpatch with a different sample rate, the argument sets the resampling method.

title: int
i
vanilla/int.description: truncate floats and store an integer

messages.description: if first element is float, stores and outputs it
store the value, non-integers are truncated (no output)

methods.description: send the stored value to a [receive] or [value] object that has the same name as the symbol (no output)

vanilla/int.body: [int] stores an integer: a float in the left inlet is truncated, stored and output, a float in the right inlet is stored without output, and a bang outputs the stored value. It can also be used to truncate floats to integers.

title: key
vanilla/key.body: [key] outputs the (system dependent) number of a "printing" key of the keyboard when it is pressed. [keyup] does the same when it is released. Check your system's preferences for 'autorepeat', as it affects the output. This only works if Pd gets the key events, which can depend on the stacking order of windows and the pointer location.

title: keyname

messages.description: 1 when key is pressed and 0 when released

vanilla/keyname.body:
keyname gives the symbolic name of the key on the right outlet, with a 1 or 0 in the left outlet if it's up or down, and works with non-printing keys like shift or "F1".

Caveat -- this only works if Pd actually gets the key events which can depend on the stacking order of windows and/or the pointer location, depending on the system.

title: keyup
vanilla/keyup.body: [keyup] outputs the (system dependent) number of a "printing" key of the keyboard when it is released. [key] does the same when it is pressed. Check your system's preferences for 'autorepeat', as it affects the output. This only works if Pd gets the key events, which can depend on the stacking order of windows and the pointer location.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/le.body: [<=] outputs 1 if its left input is less than or equal to its right input, and 0 otherwise.

title: line
vanilla/line.description: send a series of linearly stepped numbers

messages.description: set target value and start ramp
set next ramp time (cleared when ramp starts)

vanilla/line.body: [line] outputs numbers ramping linearly to a target over a given time in ms, updating at a time grain (20 ms by default). A float in the left inlet sets the target and starts the ramp, using the time set in the middle inlet; without a time it jumps to the target. 'stop' stops the ramp and 'set' sets the current value without output.

title: line~

messages.description: set target value and start ramp
set next ramp time (cleared when ramp starts)

vanilla/line~.body: The line~ object generates linear ramps whose levels and timing are determined by messages you send it. A list of two floats distributes the value over the inlets, as usual in Pd. Note that the right inlet (that sets the ramp time in milliseconds) does not remember old values (unlike every other inlet in Pd). Thus, if you don't priorly specify a time in the right inlet and sent line~ a float, it jumps immediately to the target value.

title: list append

messages.description: first list: output with the second appended, a bang is empty
second list to append, a bang clears it

vanilla/list-append.body: [list append] appends the list in its right inlet to the one in its left inlet and outputs the result. A bang in the left inlet counts as an empty list.

title: list fromsymbol

messages.description: symbol to be converted to a list of character codes

vanilla/list-fromsymbol.body:
Convert from symbols to lists of numeric character codes

[list fromsymbol] and [list tosymbol] allow you to do string manipulations (such as scanning a filename for '/' characters). They convert a list of numbers (which might be ASCII or might be unicode if, for example, they represent a filename on a non-ASCII machine) to or from a symbol.

title: list length

messages.description: messages to have its elements counted

vanilla/list-length.body:
Number of items in list.

The "list length" object outputs the number of arguments in a list or other message.

title: list prepend

messages.description: first list: output with the second prepended, a bang is empty
second list to prepend, a bang clears it

vanilla/list-prepend.body: [list prepend] prepends the list in its right inlet to the one in its left inlet and outputs the result. A bang in the left inlet counts as an empty list.

title: list split

messages.description: messages to be split into smaller lists
the first 'n' elements of the list
the remaining portion of the list
if incoming list is shorter than n

vanilla/list-split.body:
Cut a list into smaller ones.

The "list split" object takes lists and outputs the first "n" items (left outlet) and the remaining ones (middle outlet). If the incoming list also has 'n' items, the middle outlet spits a list with zero elements (which becomes a bang). The two outputs appear in the usual right-to-left order. In case there are fewer than "n" items in the list, it is output (in its entirety) from the third outlet instead. The creation argument or the inlet sets the split point.

title: list store

messages.description: output with the stored list appended, a bang outputs the stored list
set stored list (a bang is a zero element list and clears it)
the stored list, the concatenated list, or a sublist from 'get'

methods.description: prepend a list to the stored list
append a list to the stored list
output an item (if only one float is given) or sublist, where first element sets staring index and the second sets ending index (-1 is end of the list)
set values starting at index from the first element
insert values before index from the first element
delete a given item for just one float or a number of items specified in the second element starting at index from the first element (-1 means delete all items from given index)
send stored list to a named receiver

vanilla/list-store.body: put together or break apart a list to/from sublists

title: list tosymbol

messages.description: list of character codes to convert to a symbol
converted symbol from list of character codes

vanilla/list-tosymbol.body:
Convert from list of numeric character codes to symbols.

[list fromsymbol] and [list tosymbol] allow you to do string manipulations (such as scanning a filename for '/' characters). They convert a list of numbers (which might be ASCII or might be unicode if, for example, they represent a filename on a non-ASCII machine) to or from a symbol.

title: list trim

messages.description: the symbol selector is also trimmed
any other messages are output intact

vanilla/list-trim.body:
Remove list selector.

The "list trim" object inputs lists (or makes lists out of incoming non-list messages) and outputs a message whose selector is the first item of the list, and whose arguments, if any, are the remainder of the list. If the list has no items, or if its first item is numeric, the selector is "list" (which might print out as list, float, or bang.)

title: list

messages.description: first list: output with the second appended, a bang is empty
second list to append, a bang clears it

arguments.description: function of [list]: append, prepend, store, split, trim, length, fromsymbol or tosymbol

vanilla/list.body: [list] on its own is [list append]. Its first argument selects another function: append, prepend, store, split, trim, length, fromsymbol or tosymbol.

title: listbox
vanilla/listbox.body: [listbox] is a list box: it shows and outputs a list of numbers and symbols. You can type a new list, or click and drag one of its numbers to change it. 'set' changes the contents without output, and a bang outputs them.

title: loadbang
vanilla/loadbang.body:
The loadbang object outputs a 'bang' message when the containing patch is opened as a document or included in another patch as an abstraction.

Loadbangs within abstractions send their "bang" messages before those of loadbangs in the calling patch. Otherwise, the order in which the "bangs" are sent from two loadbang objects is undefined.

You can force loadbangs to fire if you send a 'loadbang' message to the patch (see 'pd-messages').

title: log

messages.description: set input value and trigger output

vanilla/log.body: As in the signal version log~, log takes a base value via an argument or the right inlet, but it defaults to e, Euler's number.

title: log~

messages.description: set base value of the log function

vanilla/log~.body: computes the logarithm of the left inlet, to the base 'e' (about 2.718), or to another base specified by the inlet or a creation argument.

title: loop~
vanilla/loop~.body:
loop~ takes input signals to set transposition and window size, and outputs a phase and a sampled window size. The window size only changes at phase zero crossings and the phase output is adjusted so that changing window size doesn't change the transposition.

You can send "bang" or "set" message to force the phase to zero--you should mute the output before doing so. This may be desirable if you've set a large window size but then want to decrease it without waiting for the next phase crossing.

title: lop~
vanilla/lop~.body: lop~ is a one-pole lowpass filter with a specified rolloff frequency. The left inlet is the incoming audio signal. The right inlet is the cutoff frequency in Hz.

title: lrshift~
vanilla/lrshift~.description: shift signal vector elements left or right
vanilla/lrshift~.body: Acting at whatever vector size the window is running at, lrshift~ shifts samples to the left (toward the beginning sample) or to the right. The argument gives the direction and the amount of the shift. The rightmost (or leftmost) samples are set to zero.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/lshift.body: [<<] shifts the bits of the left input to the left by the number of places given by the right input, which multiplies it by 2 to that power. Float inputs are truncated to integers.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/lt.body: [<] outputs 1 if its left input is less than its right input, and 0 otherwise.

title: makefilename
vanilla/makefilename.description: format a symbol with a variable field
vanilla/makefilename.body: [makefilename] formats a symbol from a format string, replacing its specifier (such as %d or %s) with the float or symbol it receives.

title: makenote
vanilla/makenote.description: send note-on and schedule note-off messages
vanilla/makenote.body: [makenote] makes MIDI-style note-on/note-off pairs: for each incoming pitch, it outputs a note-on with the current velocity and schedules a matching note-off (velocity 0) after the duration. 'stop' sends the pending note-offs right away, and 'clear' forgets them.

title: max

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/max.body: [max] outputs the larger of its left and right inputs. The right value is set by the argument or the right inlet; a float in the left inlet outputs the result, and a bang outputs it again with the stored values.

title: max~

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

arguments.description: initialize value of right inlet and makes it only take floats

vanilla/max~.body: [max~] outputs the larger of two signals. If you give a numeric argument, the right inlet only takes floats (no signals) and the argument initializes its value.

title: metro

messages.description: nonzero starts and zero stops the metronome
set metronome time for the next tempo

methods.description: set tempo value and time unit

vanilla/metro.body: [metro] sends bangs at regular time intervals. A bang or nonzero float starts it, and 0 or 'stop' stops it. The interval is set by the argument or the right inlet, in milliseconds by default, which the 'tempo' message or the 2nd and 3rd arguments can change.

title: midiin

messages.description: raw MIDI byte by byte (except real-time messages)

vanilla/midiin.body: [midiin] outputs raw MIDI input byte by byte, except real-time messages, with the port number on the right outlet.

title: midiout
vanilla/midiout.body: [midiout] sends raw MIDI output, byte by byte or as packet lists, so it can send any MIDI message, including real-time and sysex ones. The right inlet sets the port number.

title: midirealtimein
vanilla/midirealtimein.body: [midirealtimein] outputs MIDI real-time messages, such as clock, start and stop, with the port number on the right outlet.

title: min

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/min.body: [min] outputs the smaller of its left and right inputs. The right value is set by the argument or the right inlet; a float in the left inlet outputs the result, and a bang outputs it again with the stored values.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/minus.body: [-] subtracts the right input from the left one. The right value is set by the argument or the right inlet; a float in the left inlet outputs the result, and a bang outputs it again with the stored values.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

arguments.description: initialize value of right inlet and makes it only take floats

vanilla/minus~.body: [-~] subtracts the right signal from the left one. If you give a numeric argument, the right inlet only takes floats (no signals) and the argument initializes its value.

title: min~

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

arguments.description: initialize value of right inlet and makes it only take floats

vanilla/min~.body: [min~] outputs the smaller of two signals. If you give a numeric argument, the right inlet only takes floats (no signals) and the argument initializes its value.

title: mod

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/mod.body: [mod] does integer division and outputs the remainder (modulus). [div] outputs the integer quotient.

title: moses

messages.description: input number if less than control value
input number if equal or higher than control value

vanilla/moses.body: Moses takes numbers and outputs them at left if they're less than a control value,  and at right if they're greater or equal to it.

title: msg

methods.description: add message terminating by a semicolon
add message without the terminating semicolon
add a dollar-sign symbol that starts with a float

vanilla/msg.body: [msg] is a message box: it holds one or more messages and sends them out when clicked or when it gets a message, replacing $1, $2... with the elements of that message. Messages after a semicolon go to the receive name given by their first element. 'set' replaces the contents, and 'add', 'add2', 'addcomma' and 'addsemi' append to them.

title: mtof
vanilla/mtof.body: Takes a MIDI value as input and outputs the corresponding frequency value at A=440

title: mtof~
vanilla/mtof~.description: MIDI to frequency conversion for signals
vanilla/mtof~.body: Takes a MIDI signal as input and outputs the corresponding frequency signal at A=440

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/mul.body: [*] multiplies its left and right inputs. The right value is set by the argument or the right inlet; a float in the left inlet outputs the result, and a bang outputs it again with the stored values.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

arguments.description: initialize value of right inlet and makes it only take floats

vanilla/mul~.body: [*~] multiplies two signals. If you give a numeric argument, the right inlet only takes floats (no signals) and the argument initializes its value.

title: namecanvas
vanilla/namecanvas.description: attach the canvas window to a name
vanilla/namecanvas.body: You can use namecanvas to attach a receive name to a canvas (patch window) so you can send it messages (useful for 'dynamic patching').

title: nbx
my_numbox
vanilla/nbx.description: number box with a range, log scaling and its own appearance

methods.description: sets vertical range in pixels for the log mode
sets font type <0: DejaVu Sans Mono, 1: Helvetica, 2: Times> and font size
first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)
sets position in the patch canvas
changes the position by a x/y delta in pixels

vanilla/nbx.body: [nbx] is a number box GUI with more options than the plain number box: a range, linear or logarithmic dragging, an initial value, a label and its own colors. Click and drag, or type, to output a value. Incoming floats set the value and are passed through, 'set' sets it without output, and a bang outputs it.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/neq.body: [!=] outputs 1 if its left input is not equal to its right input, and 0 otherwise.

title: netreceive
vanilla/netreceive.description: listen for incoming messages from network

messages.description: messages sent from connected netsend objects
address and port (only with the -f flag)

flags.name: -f
flags.description: flag for from address & port outlet

methods.description: a number sets or changes the port number (0 or negative closes the port). Optional symbol is a hostname which can be a UDP multicast address or a network interface
sends messages back to connected netsend objects

vanilla/netreceive.body: [netreceive] listens on a network port for messages from [netsend] objects or other software, over TCP by default or UDP with -u, and outputs them. With TCP, the middle outlet reports the number of open connections, and 'send' sends messages back to them. With -b, messages are received as lists of bytes.

title: netsend
vanilla/netsend.description: send Pd messages over a network

messages.description: nonzero if connection is open, zero otherwise
messages sent back from netreceive objects

methods.description: sets host and port number, an additional port argument can be set for messages sent back from the receiver

vanilla/netsend.body: [netsend] sends messages over the network to a [netreceive] object or other software, over TCP by default or UDP with -u. 'connect' takes a host name or address and a port, 'send' sends a message, and the left outlet is 1 while connected. With -b, messages are sent as lists of bytes.

title: noise~

messages.description: set seed for random number generator
white noise signal (in the range from -1 to 1)

vanilla/noise~.body: Noise~ is a random number generator that outputs white noise from a pseudo-random number generator at the audio rate (with output from -1 to 1).

title: notein
vanilla/notein.body: [notein] outputs MIDI note messages: the note number, velocity and channel. A release comes out as velocity 0. It listens on all channels by default; an argument sets the channel and removes the channel outlet. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: noteout
vanilla/noteout.body: [noteout] sends MIDI note messages: a note number and velocity, on the channel set by the argument or the right inlet (channel 1 by default). A velocity of 0 is a note-off. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: openpanel

messages.description: open dialog window to choose file(s) or directory
set starting directory and open dialog window

arguments.description: mode: 0 for a file (default), 1 for a directory, 2 for multiple files

vanilla/openpanel.body:
When openpanel gets a "bang", a file browser appears on the screen. By default, if you select a file, its name appears on the outlet

A mode argument allow you to select a directory or multiple files.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/or.body: [|] outputs the bitwise OR of its left and right inputs: each bit of the result is 1 where that bit is 1 in either input. Float inputs are truncated to integers. For a logical (Boolean) OR, use [||].

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/oror.body: [||] outputs 1 if either its left or its right input is nonzero, and 0 otherwise (a logical OR). Inputs are truncated to integers, so 0.5 counts as zero. A bang evaluates the operation again.

messages.description: one or more channels to the left side of operation
one or more channels to the right side of operation
sets the right side value, floats only with an argument
one or more channels with the result of the operation

arguments.description: initializes right inlet's value and impedes signal connections

vanilla/oror~.body: [||~] performs a logical OR on signals: for each sample, it outputs 1 if the left or the right input is nonzero, and 0 if both are zero.

title: oscformat
vanilla/oscformat.description: OSC messages to and from Pd lists

messages.description: list to format into an OSC packet

arguments.description: list of one or more addresses

flags.name: -f <symbol>
flags.description: sets format as in the 'format' message

vanilla/oscformat.body:
[oscformat] makes OSC (Open Sound Control) packets, byte by byte, suitable for sending over the network with [netsend] in UDP binary mode. The OSC address (the strings between the slashes) is given by the creation arguments or by "set" messages.

If a format is given (with the -f flag or the 'format' message), it interprets incoming data as integer, float, string or 'blob'. Blobs are given as an atom count followed by that number of elements; if the count is negative, the entire remaining message is included. Elements left over at the end of the format string get the default float and symbol conversions.

title: oscparse
vanilla/oscparse.description: OSC messages to and from Pd lists

messages.description: OSC packet to convert to Pd list messages
Pd list messages from OSC packets
split point for address and message

flags.name: -n
flags.description: interpret floats in addresses as floats

vanilla/oscparse.body:
[oscparse] takes lists of numbers, interpreting them as the bytes of an OSC (Open Sound Control) message, and outputs a list with first the symbols making up the OSC address, then the numbers and symbols in the message.

There's no way to tell floats from integers, nor to see blobs unambiguously. If it receives a bundle, it parses all the messages in it in the order they appear, and ignores the bundle's time tag.

title: osc~

messages.description: cosine waveform (in the range of -1 to 1)

vanilla/osc~.body: The osc~ object outputs a cosine wave. The frequency input can be either a float or a signal. The right inlet resets the phase with values from 0 to 1 (where '1' is the same as '0' and '0.5' is half the cycle).

title: outlet

messages.description: any message to send to parent patch

vanilla/outlet.body: [outlet] creates an outlet on the box of the subpatch or abstraction it is in, and sends out the messages it receives. Outlets are ordered from left to right by their position.

title: outlet~

messages.description: signal to send to parent patch

arguments.description: downsampling method. 'hold' for sample/hold, 'pad' for zero-padded and 'lin' for linear interpolation

vanilla/outlet~.body: [outlet~] creates a signal outlet on the box of the subpatch or abstraction it is in, and sends the signal it receives out of it. In a subpatch with a different sample rate, the argument sets the resampling method.

title: output~
vanilla/output~.body:
This is a very simple abstraction that is widely used in Pd's documentation (help files and examples). It is included here just for convenience.

Output~ takes a stereo signal and has GUI controls to set the volume gain and mute it. The number box sets the output gain in dB (from 0 to 100) and whenever you click on it to drag it, the DSP engine is turned on. The mute bang turns the volume off (sets to 0) but restores to the last setting when you click back on it to unmute.

The left inlet also takes a bang message to mute/unmute and a 'level' message to control the level output in dB.

It communicates with this one through audio channels and messages: 'pd~ start' with a patch name starts it, other messages are sent to objects in it, and its [stdout] objects send messages back. The -ninsig and -noutsig flags set the number of signal channels.

vanilla/percent.body: [%] outputs the remainder of a division, like [mod], but acts differently for negative inputs (and might act variously depending on CPU design). It is provided for back compatibility.

vanilla/pgmin.body: [pgmin] outputs program change numbers from MIDI input, with their channel. Known bug: program change values in [pgmin] and [pgmout] are indexed from 1, so they go from 1 to 128, not 0 to 127.

vanilla/pgmout.body: [pgmout] sends program changes to MIDI output, on the given channel. Known bug: program change values in [pgmin] and [pgmout] are indexed from 1, so they go from 1 to 128, not 0 to 127.

title: phasor~

messages.description: phase ramp (in the range of 0 to 1)

vanilla/phasor~.body:
The phasor~ object outputs phase ramps whose values are from 0 to 1 and it repeats this cycle depending on the frequency input. It looks like a sawtooth signal but it's traditionally used for table lookup via cos~ or tabread4~. The frequency input can be either a float or a signal. Positive frequency values generate upwards ramps and negative values generate downwards ramps.

The right inlet resets the phase with values from 0 to 1 (where '1' is the same as '0' and '0.5' is half the cycle).

title: pipe

sets delay time in ms, always the last argument

vanilla/pipe.body:
Message "delay line"

The [pipe] object stores a sequence of messages and outputs them after a specified delay time in milliseconds. The output is scheduled when storing the incoming message. Thus changing the delay time doesn't affect the messages that are already scheduled.

You can specify the data type with a first argument (which is a float by default). A symbol argument "s", "f", or "p" specifies a "symbol", "float" (number), or pointer type. The delay time comes then as the last argument.

You can specify compound messages (lists) by adding more than one argument.

title: pique

messages.description: FFT size, real and imaginary table names, and maximum number of peaks
partial index, frequency in Hz, amplitude, cosine and sine components

NOTE: pique is obsolete! consider using [sigmund~]

pique takes unwindowed FFT analyses as input (they should be stored in arrays) and outputs a list of peaks, giving their peak number, frequency, amplitude, and phase (as a cosine/sine pair.)

Its arguments set the field, color, line width, position and x spacing; the array elements are also drawn with their own template's drawing instructions.

A bang outputs it, and 'traverse' and 'next' move it through the scalars of a patch, each going out the outlet for its template; the rightmost outlet bangs at the end of the list. Pointers are safe: when a scalar is deleted, pointers to it become invalid instead of pointing at freed memory.

title: poly
vanilla/poly.body: The poly object takes a stream of pitch/velocity pairs and outputs triples containing voice number, pitch and velocity. You can pack the output and use the route object to route messages among a bank of voices depending on the first outlet. Another option is to connect it [clone] so you can route to different copies. Poly can be configured to do voice stealing or not (the default.

title: polytouchin
vanilla/polytouchin.body: [polytouchin] outputs MIDI polyphonic aftertouch: the aftertouch value, note number and channel. It listens on all channels by default; an argument sets the channel and removes the channel outlet. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: polytouchout
vanilla/polytouchout.body: [polytouchout] sends MIDI polyphonic aftertouch: a value for a note number, on the channel set by the argument or the right inlet. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: pow

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/pow.body: Pow raises a number on the left inlet to a numeric power (given by the right inlet or argument). Like the signal version, pow has protection against NaNs, which become 0.

title: powtodb
vanilla/powtodb.body: [powtodb] converts power units, equal to the square of the "RMS" amplitude, to dB, so that a power of 1 corresponds to 100 dB and 1e-10 to 0 dB. Values below 1e-10 are clipped to 0 dB. [dbtopow] does the reverse.

title: powtodb~
vanilla/powtodb~.body: [powtodb~] converts a signal in power units (the square of the "RMS" amplitude) to dB, sample by sample, so that a power of 1 corresponds to 100 dB and 1e-10 to 0 dB. Values below 1e-10 are clipped to 0 dB.

title: pow~

messages.description: set numeric power to raise to

vanilla/pow~.body:
pow~ raises a signal to a numeric power (given by another signal or argument/float). The inputs may be positive, zero, or negative.

WARNING: it's easy to generate "infinity" by accident, and if you do, the DSP chain may dramatically slow down if you're using an i386 or ia64 processor. Out-of-range floating point values are thousands of times slower to compute with than in-range ones. There' a protection against NaNs (they become 0).

title: print

messages.description: any message to print into the terminal window

arguments.description: message to distinct one [print] from another

vanilla/print.body:
Print prints out the messages it receives on the "terminal window" that Pd is run from. If no argument is given,  the message has a "print:" prefix. Any message as an argument is used as the prefix instead (so you can differentiate between different printouts).

You can also do command/control + click on the terminal window and the corresponding [print] object will be selected in your patch.

title: print~
vanilla/print~.description: print out raw values of a signal

messages.description: signal block to print on terminal window
print one block on terminal window
sets and prints number of blocks on terminal window

arguments.description: symbol to distinct one [print~] from another

vanilla/print~.body: The print~ object takes a signal input and prints one or more blocks (or 'vectors') out when you send it a bang or a number. By default a block is 64 samples.

title: q8_rsqrt~

messages.description: input to reciprocal square root function
output of reciprocal square root function

vanilla/q8_rsqrt~.body:
q8_rsqrt~, is included in Pd for back compatibility but should probably not be used. It only gives about 8 bit accuracy.

Use [rsqrt~].

title: q8_sqrt~
vanilla/q8_sqrt~.body:
q8_sqrt~ is included in Pd for back compatibility but should probably not be used. It only gives about 8 bit accuracy.

Use [sqrt~].

title: qlist

messages.description: list of leading numbers for the next message
when reaching the end of sequence

methods.description: single-step forward, optional float suppresses message sending
add a message to a qlist
add a message to a qlist but don't terminate it

vanilla/qlist.body:
The qlist object reads text files containing time-tagged Pd messages. You can have them sequenced automatically (by sending a "bang" message, possibly changing speed via "tempo" messages) or manually via the "rewind" and "next" messages.

To run the qlist automatically, send it a "read" message (the filename is relative to the directory the patch is in) and later a "bang." Messages in the file are separated by semicolons. Optional leading numbers are delay times in milliseconds. If the tempo is different from 1 the messages are sent faster or slower accordingly. Messages should start with a symbol giving the destination object.

To run it manually, send "rewind" followed by "next". All messages not preceded by numbers are sent. As soon as a message starting with one or more numbers is encountered, the numbers are output as a list. There are many ways you could design a sequencer around this.

You can also record textual messages and save them to a file. Send "clear" to empty the qlist and "add" to add messages (terminated with semicolons.) The message, "add2" adds a list of atoms without finishing with a semicolon in case you want to make variable-length messages.

title: random

messages.description: set the range and output a random value

methods.description: set a seed value for repeatable random numbers

vanilla/random.body:
Random outputs pseudo random integers from 0 to N-1 where N is the creation argument. You can specify a seed if you wish. Seeds are kept locally so that if two Randoms are seeded the same they will have the same output (or indeed you can seed the same one twice to repeat the output.)

On the other hand, if you don't supply a seed, each instance of random gets its own seed. Nothing is known about the quality of the pseudo random number generator: it isn't any standard one.

messages.description: channel output of a given file

arguments.description: per channel buffer size in bytes

flags.name: -m

vanilla/readsf~.body: [readsf~] plays a soundfile from disk into its signal outputs. Open the file with the 'open' message a couple of seconds before you need it, then start playback with 'start' or a nonzero float.

title: realtime
vanilla/realtime.body:
Ask OS for elapsed real time.

The realtime object measures elapsed real time,  as measured by your operating system.

title: receive
r

messages.description: sets the receive name (if created without arguments)

vanilla/receive.body: The [receive] object gets messages directly from [send] or other objects like [list store], [float], [int] and [value] via a 'send' method.

title: receive~
r~
vanilla/receive~.description: receive a signal from a matching [send~]

messages.description: outputs signal from a matching send~ object

vanilla/receive~.body:
A send~ object copies its input to a local buffer which all receive~ objects of the same name read from. They may be in different windows or even different patches. Any number of receives may be associated with one send~ but it is an error to have two send~s of the same name. Receive~ takes "set" messages to switch between send~s.
Multi channel connections is supported.
Send~/Receive~ only work for the default block size (64). For FFT applications, see also [tabsend~] and [tabreceive~].

title: rev1~
vanilla/rev1~.body:
This is an experimental reverberator design composed of a series of allpass filters with exponentially growing delay times. Each allpass filter has a gain of 0.7. The reverb time is adjusted by adjusting the input gains of the allpass filters. The last unit is modified so that its first two "echos" mimic those of an allpass but its loop gain depends on reverb time.

Reverb time is controlled by specifying the dB gain (100 normal) after one second, so that 100 corresponds to infinite reverb time, 70 to two seconds, 40 to one second, and 0 to 0

The "clear" button impolitely clears out all the delay lines, You may immediately resume pumping the reverberator, but the input signal should be cleanly enveloped. The output, too, must be enveloped and may not be opened until 5 ms after the "clear" message is sent.

The rev1~ module eats about 18% of my 300mHz P2 machine.

title: rev2~
vanilla/rev2~.body: [rev2~] is a reverberator based on a feedback delay network, with one input and four outputs. The arguments or inlets set the output level in dB, the liveness (the internal feedback, 100 for infinite reverb), the crossover frequency and the high frequency damping: above the crossover, the feedback is reduced by the damping percentage.

title: rev3~
vanilla/rev3~.body: [rev3~] is a bigger reverberator than [rev2~], with two inputs and four outputs, a larger feedback delay network and an early reflections stage. The arguments or inlets set the output level in dB, the liveness (the internal feedback, 100 for infinite reverb), the crossover frequency and the high frequency damping.

title: rfft~

messages.description: time domain real signal to transform
real part of frequency domain signal
imaginary part of frequency domain signal

vanilla/rfft~.body:
[rfft~] does a forward Fourier analysis of a real signal. It outputs N/2+1 real parts and N/2-1 imaginary parts, and the other outputs are zero: at DC and at the Nyquist frequency there is no imaginary part.

The analysis size is one block, which you can set with [block~] or [switch~]. There is no normalization, so an FFT followed by an IFFT has a gain of N.

title: rifft~

messages.description: real part of frequency domain signal
imaginary part of frequency domain signal
real part of frequency domain signal

vanilla/rifft~.body:
[rifft~] does an inverse Fourier transform back to a real signal, from the real and imaginary parts of a spectrum as [rfft~] outputs them.

The analysis size is one block, which you can set with [block~] or [switch~]. There is no normalization, so an FFT followed by an IFFT has a gain of N.

title: rmstodb
vanilla/rmstodb.body: [rmstodb] converts linear ("RMS") amplitude to dB. dB in Pd are dBFS with an offset of 100, so an RMS of 1 corresponds to 100 dB and 1e-05 to 0 dB. Values below 1e-05 (down to 0, which is minus infinity dB) are clipped to 0 dB. [dbtorms] does the reverse.

title: rmstodb~
vanilla/rmstodb~.body: [rmstodb~] converts a signal in linear ("RMS") amplitude to dB, sample by sample, so that an RMS of 1 corresponds to 100 dB and 1e-05 to 0 dB. Values below 1e-05 are clipped to 0 dB.

title: route
vanilla/route.description: route messages according to first element

messages.description: message to route according to first element
when input doesn't match the arguments it's passed here

arguments.description: of floats or symbols to route to to

vanilla/route.body: [route] checks the first element of a message against its arguments: when one matches, the rest of the message goes out the matching outlet, and otherwise the whole message goes out the rightmost outlet. The arguments can be numbers or symbols, but not a mix of the two.

title: rpole~

methods.description: clear internal state to zero (same as "set 0")

vanilla/rpole~.body:
Rpole~ filters an audio signal (left inlet) via a raw one-pole (recursive) real filter, whose coefficient is controlled by a creation argument or by an audio signal (right inlet).

The action of rpole~ is:
y[n] = x[n] + a[n] * y[n-1]
where y[n] is the output, x[n] the input, and a[n] the filter coefficient. The filter is unstable if/when |a[n]| > 1.

The transfer function is H(Z) = 1/(1 - aZ^-1).

Pd also provides a suite of user-friendly filters. This and other raw filters are provided for situations which the user-friendly ones can't handle. See Chapter 8 of http://msp.ucsd.edu/techniques/latest/book-html/node127.html for an introduction to the necessary theory.

messages.description: set value on left-hand side and trigger output

vanilla/rshift.body: [>>] shifts the bits of the left input to the right by the number of places given by the right input, which divides it by 2 to that power, rounding down. The shift is signed, so negative numbers stay negative. Float inputs are truncated to integers.

title: rsqrt~

messages.description: input to reciprocal square root function
output of reciprocal square root function

vanilla/rsqrt~.body:
rsqrt~ takes the approximate reciprocal square root of the incoming signal (the same as '1/sqrt(input) using a fast approximate algorithm which is probably accurate to about 120 dB (20 bits)

An older object, q8_rsqrt~, is included in Pd for back compatibility but should probably not be used. It only gives about 8 bit accuracy.

title: rzero_rev~

methods.description: clear internal state to zero (same as "set 0")

vanilla/rzero_rev~.body:
Rzero_rev~ filters an audio signal (left inlet) via a raw one-zero (non-recursive) real filter, whose coefficient is controlled by a creation argument or by an audio signal (right inlet). The impulse response is that of [rzero~] reversed in time.

The action of rzero_rev~ is:
y[n] = -a[n] * x[n] + x[n-1]
where y[n] is the output, x[n] the input, and a[n] the filter coefficient. The filter is always stable.

The transfer function is H(Z) = -a + Z^-1.

Pd also provides a suite of user-friendly filters. This and other raw filters are provided for situations which the user-friendly ones can't handle. See Chapter 8 of http://msp.ucsd.edu/techniques/latest/book-html/node127.html for an introduction to the necessary theory.

title: rzero~

methods.description: clear internal state to zero (same as "set 0")

vanilla/rzero~.body:
Rzero~ filters an audio signal (left inlet) via a raw one-zero (non-recursive) real filter, whose coefficient is controlled by a creation argument or by an audio signal (right inlet).

The action of rzero~ is:
y[n] = x[n] - a[n] * x[n-1]
where y[n] is the output, x[n] the input, and a[n] the filter coefficient. The filter is always stable.

The transfer function is H(Z) = 1 - aZ^-1.

Pd also provides a suite of user-friendly filters. This and other raw filters are provided for situations which the user-friendly ones can't handle. See Chapter 8 of http://msp.ucsd.edu/techniques/latest/book-html/node127.html for an introduction to the necessary theory.

title: samphold~

messages.description: control signal (triggers when smaller than previous)

methods.description: set last value of right inlet
set last value of right inlet to infinity (forces output)

vanilla/samphold~.body:
The samphold~ object samples its left input whenever its right input decreases in value (as a phasor~ does each period, for example.) Both inputs are audio signals.

The "set" message sets the output value (which gets updated normally afterward.) The "reset" message causes samphold~ to act as if the given value were the most recent value of the control (right) input. Use this, for example, if you reset the incoming phasor but don't want the jump reflected in the output. Plain "reset" is equivalent to "reset infinity" which forces the next input to be sampled.

title: samplerate~
vanilla/samplerate~.body: When sent a 'bang' message, samplerate~ outputs the current audio sample rate. If called within a subwindow that is up- or down-sampled, the sample rate of signals within that subwindow are reported.

title: savepanel
vanilla/savepanel.description: query you for the name of a file to create

messages.description: open dialog window to choose a file name to save to
set starting directory and open dialog window

vanilla/savepanel.body: When savepanel gets a "bang" a "Save As" file browser appears on the screen, If you choose a filename, it appears on the outlet

title: savestate
vanilla/savestate.description: save and restore run-time state from within an abstraction

messages.description: one or more list when the parent patch gets saved
one or more list when the parent patch is opened
when the parent patch is saved

vanilla/savestate.body:
The savestate object is used inside abstractions to save their state as they are used in a calling (parent) patch. When the parent patch (such as this one, which calls the "savestate-example" abstraction) is saved, the included savestate object sends a 'bang' message out its right outlet, with which the abstraction may respond by presenting one or more 'list' messages back to the 'savestate' object. These lists are saved as part of the calling patch. If the calling patch is reopened later, the lists are sent out the left outlet of the savestate object. The abstraction can then use them to restore its state.

Note that abstractions within 'clone' objects are not handled!

The abstraction may itself be modified at will without disturbing the saved states of its copies in any calling patches, as long as the usage of the saved and restored lists is kept compatible.

The saved messages are output when the object is recreated, before any outside connections are made and possibly before other parts of a saved patch have been restored. You can use a "loadbang" object to send messages to objects elsewhere in the owning patch at load time once the entire patch is loaded.

Multiple savestate objects aren't differentiated, so they all receive all lists sent to any one of them and output them.

Hint: 'text' objects can be saved/restored using 'text tolist' and 'text fromlist'.

vanilla/scalar-define.body: [scalar define] defines and maintains a scalar of the template given as argument. A bang outputs a pointer to it, and with the -k flag its contents are saved with the patch.

sel

vanilla/send.body: [Send] sends messages to "receive" objects. Sends and receives are named to tell them whom to connect to. They work across windows too.

title: send~
s~
vanilla/send~.description: send a signal to matching [receive~] objects

messages.description: signal to send to matching receive~ object(s)

methods.description: sets number of channels to send

vanilla/send~.body:
A send~ object copies its input to a local buffer which all receive~ objects of the same name read from. They may be in different windows or even different patches. Any number of receives may be associated with one send~ but it is an error to have two send~s of the same name. Receive~ takes "set" messages to switch between send~s.
Multi channel connections is supported.
Send~/Receive~ only work for the default block size (64). For FFT applications, see also [tabsend~] and [tabreceive~].

title: set

messages.description: set values with previously given data (leftmost inlet only)

arguments.description: symbols for field names (each creates an inlet)

flags.name: -symbol
flags.description: so you can set symbol values

methods.description: if none or just one field is given, you can use 'set' to set struct name and field

vanilla/set.body:
"Set" takes a pointer to a scalar in its rightmost inlet. The remaining inlets set numeric fields. Arrays are accessed using the "element" object, and lists using "text" objects. Only the leftmost inlet is "hot".

To set fields whose values are symbols, give the set object the "-symbol" argument. (Unfortunately, you can't mix symbols and numbers in the same "set" object.)

You can use the template "-" as a wild card (this may be slower than if you use a specific template name). Also, if there are zero or one fields specified, you can send a "set" message to set a new template name and field name.

title: setsize

messages.description: pointer to a scalar with an array field

vanilla/setsize.body: [setsize] sets the number of elements of an array field in a scalar. The right inlet takes a pointer to the scalar, the arguments give its template and array field, and a float in the left inlet sets the size. The smallest size is 1; shrinking loses the extra elements and growing fills the new ones with zeros.

title: siginfo~

messages.description: signal information as messages, or one outlet per argument keyword

arguments.description: keywords choosing the outlets: dspstate, blocksize, channels, overlap, samplerate, samplespersecond

vanilla/siginfo~.body: [siginfo~] reports the dspstate, blocksize, number of channels, overlap factor, samplerate and the number of samples processed per second (which is the sample rate times the overlap) of the signal connected to it. Most information (with the exception of the number of channels) is the same for all signals within a window.

title: sigmund~

messages.description: with -t: table name, points, first point, sample rate, debug flag

vanilla/sigmund~.body: [sigmund~] analyzes a sound into sinusoidal components, which it can report individually or combine into a pitch estimate. The arguments choose its outlets: pitch, notes, env (amplitude), peaks and tracks. Flags and messages set the analysis parameters, and with -t it analyzes an array instead of its signal input.

vanilla/slash~.body: [/~] divides the left signal by the right one. If you give a numeric argument, the right inlet only takes floats (no signals) and the argument initializes its value.

maximum upward slew of linear region

vanilla/slop~.body: [slop~] is a lowpass filter whose response speed depends on its state, useful for slew limiting, dynamics processing (companders, limiters, noise gates) and soft saturation. Within a linear region it is a one-pole lowpass at the given cutoff; beyond the maximum upward and downward slews, its cutoff tends to separate asymptotic values.

the converted signal at every bang

vanilla/snapshot~.body:
The snapshot~ object takes a signal and converts it to a control value whenever it receives a bang in its left outlet. This object is particularly useful for monitoring outputs.

A 'set' message is provided for the (rare) situations where you might make a known change to the signal input, and then read snapshot's value before any ensuing signal computation.

methods.description: reads a file into one or more arrays, one per channel; optional flags: -wave, -aiff, -caf, -next, -skip <float>, -resize, -maxsize <float>, -ascii, -raw <list>

vanilla/soundfiler.body:
The soundfiler object reads and writes floating point arrays to binary soundfiles which may contain uncompressed 2- or 3-byte integer ("pcm") or 4-byte floating point samples in wave, aiff, caf, next, or ascii text formats. The number of channels of the soundfile need not match the number of arrays given (extras are dropped and unsupplied channels are zeroed out).

The number of channels is limited to 64.

Flags for 'read' messages:
- -wave, -aiff, -caf, -next
- -skip <sample frames to skip in file>
- -resize (resizes arrays to the size of the sound file)
- -maxsize <maximum number of samples we can resize to>
- -raw <headersize> <channels> <bytespersample> <endianness>: ignores all header and type information, instead of letting soundfiler figure out which of the known soundfile formats the file belongs to. Endianness is "l" ("little") for Intel machines or "b" ("big") for older PPC Macintoshes. You can give "n" (natural) to take the byte order your machine prefers.
- -ascii: reads a file containing ascii numbers. May be combined with -resize. Newlines in the file are ignored, and non-numeric fields are replaced by zero. If multiple arrays are specified, the first elements of each array should come first in the file, followed by all the second elements and so on (interleaved).

Flags for 'write' messages:
- -wave, -aiff, -caf, -next, -ascii
- -big, -little (sample endianness)
- -skip <number of sample frames to skip in array>
- -nframes <maximum number to write>
- -bytes <2, 3, or 4>
- -normalize
- -rate <sample rate>

any input message if spigot is opened

vanilla/spigot.body: Spigot passes messages from its left inlet to its outlet,  as long as a nonzero number is sent to its right inlet. When its right inlet gets zero,  incoming messages are "blocked" i.e.,  ignored.

title: sqrt
vanilla/sqrt.body: [sqrt] outputs the square root of its input. Negative inputs output 0.

title: sqrt~
vanilla/sqrt~.body:
sqrt~ takes the approximate square root of the incoming signal, using a fast, approximate algorithm which is probably accurate to about 120 dB (20 bits).

An older object, q8_sqrt~, is included in Pd for back compatibility but should probably not be used. It only gives about 8 bit accuracy.

title: stdout

flags.name: -flush
flags.description: flush the output after each message (default on W32)

flags.name: -noflush
flags.description: do not flush the output after each message

vanilla/stdout.body: The 'stdout' object is useful in conjunction with the pd~ object, which starts a Pd sub-process. Messages sent to the sub-process standard output appear on the left output of the pd~ object in the owning process. This might also be useful in other situations. Note that there's no corresponding "stdin" object - there seems to be no one canonical way such a thing should act.

title: stripnote

messages.description: MIDI velocity (no output if equal to zero)

vanilla/stripnote.body:
Stripnote ignores note-off (zero-velocity) messages from a stream of MIDI-style note message and passes the others through unchanged. It can deal with any kind of number (negative,  floats,  whatever) even though MIDI values need to be integers from 0 to 127!

The left inlet takes the note number and the right inlet takes velocity values. Alternatively,  you can send it a list that spreads the values through the inlets.

This is very useful if you want a Note-On message to trigger something in Pd but you don't want a Note-Off to trigger anything when you release the note.

title: struct
vanilla/struct.description: declare the fields in a data structure

messages.description: select, deselect, click, displace and change notifications

arguments.description: template name plus types and names of given fields (array fields also need the array's template name)

methods.description: add a scalar of this template to the named window (prefixed with 'pd', as in 'pd-data'), optionally followed by field names and values

vanilla/struct.body: There should be one "struct" object in each Pd window you are using as a data structure template. The arguments specify the types and names of the fields. For array fields, a third argument specifies the template that the array elements should belong to

title: swap
fswap

messages.description: set left value, swap and output
set left value, swap and output

vanilla/swap.body: The swap object swaps the positions of two incoming numbers. The number coming in through the right inlet will be sent to the left outlet and the number coming in left will come out right. Only the left inlet is hot and triggers output on both outlets. Output order is right to left as in [trigger].

title: switch~
vanilla/switch~.description: set block size and on/off control for DSP

messages.description: nonzero turns DSP on, zero turns DSP off
when turned off, computes just one DSP cycle

vanilla/switch~.body: [switch~] sets the block size, overlap and up/downsampling of the window it is in, like [block~], and can also switch DSP on and off for that window: a nonzero float turns it on and 0 off. While it is off, a bang computes one DSP cycle.

messages.description: gets converted to symbol, stored, and output
stores the received symbol and outputs it

title: symbolbox
vanilla/symbolbox.body: [symbolbox] is a symbol box: it shows and outputs a symbol. Click it, type a symbol and hit enter to output it. 'set' changes the symbol without output, and a bang outputs it.

title: sysexin

messages.description: MIDI system exclusive messages only, byte by byte

vanilla/sysexin.body: [sysexin] outputs MIDI system exclusive messages byte by byte, with the port number on the right outlet.

title: table
vanilla/table.body: [table] creates a subpatch with an array of the given name and size. Unlike [array define], it doesn't save the array contents with the patch.

title: tabosc4~

methods.description: set table name with the waveform

vanilla/tabosc4~.body:
tabosc4~ is a traditional computer music style wavetable lookup oscillator using 4-point polynomial interpolation. The table should have a power of two points plus three "guard points", one at the beginning and two at the end, which should be wraparound copies of the last point and the first two points, respectively. The "sinesum" and "cosinesum" methods for arrays do this automatically for you if you just want to specify partial strengths.

For good results use 512 points for up to about 15 partials, or 32*npartials (rounded up to a power of 2) for more than 15 partials. Don't send new "sinesum" messages to tables while you're running; instead, use "set" messages to switch between tables.

The frequency input can be either a float or a signal. The right inlet resets the phase with values from 0 to 1 (where '1' is the same as '0' and '0.5' is half the cycle).

title: tabplay~
vanilla/tabplay~.description: play a table as a sample (non-transposing)

messages.description: sets starting sample and plays the sample
starting sample and duration in samples
bang when finished playing the table

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

methods.description: set the table with the sample

vanilla/tabplay~.body: The tabplay~ object plays a sample, or part of one, with no transposition or interpolation. It is cheaper than tabread4~ and there are none of tabread4~'s interpolation artifacts.

title: tabread
vanilla/tabread.description: read a number from a table

messages.description: sets table index and output its value

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

vanilla/tabread.body: The tabread object reads values from an array ("table") according to an index. The index is rounded down to the next lower integer. Values in the table correspond to indices starting at 0. Indices outside of the range are replaced by the nearest index in range.

title: tabread4

messages.description: sets table index and output its value with interpolation

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

vanilla/tabread4.body: [tabread4] reads values from an array with four-point polynomial interpolation, so fractional indexes give values in between the elements. Indexes should range from 1 to the array size minus 2 for the interpolation to be meaningful. 'set' changes the array.

title: tabread4~

messages.description: sets table index and output its value with interpolation

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

vanilla/tabread4~.body: [tabread4~] reads an array with four-point polynomial interpolation, using a signal as the index, which makes it suitable for building samplers. The right inlet sets an onset added to the index, for precise indexing into large arrays. Indexes should range from 1 to the array size minus 2.

title: tabread~

messages.description: sets table index and output its value

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

vanilla/tabread~.body: Tabread~ looks up values out of the named array. Incoming values are truncated to the next lower integer, and values out of bounds get the nearest (first or last) point.

title: tabreceive~
vanilla/tabreceive~.description: read a block of a signal from arrays continuously

messages.description: outputs 1 or more channels from matching arrays

vanilla/tabreceive~.body: [tabreceive~] continuously outputs one block from an array every DSP cycle, such as one written by [tabsend~]. A block is 64 samples by default, which [block~] can change.

title: tabsend~
vanilla/tabsend~.description: write a block of a signal to arrays continuously

messages.description: 1 or more channels to write to corresponding arrays

vanilla/tabsend~.body: [tabsend~] continuously writes one block of its signal input to an array, every DSP cycle, for [tabreceive~] to read back. A block is 64 samples by default, which [block~] can change.

title: tabwrite
vanilla/tabwrite.description: write a number to a table

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

vanilla/tabwrite.body: Tabwrite writes floats into an array,  input values are set in the left inlet,  while the index is set on the right inlet.

title: tabwrite~
vanilla/tabwrite~.description: write a signal in an array

messages.description: signal to write to an array

arguments.description: sets table name with the sample

vanilla/tabwrite~.body: [tabwrite~] records a signal into an array. A bang writes from the beginning to the end of the array, 'start' with a number starts at that index, and 'stop' stops recording. 'set' changes the array.

title: tan
vanilla/tan.body: [tan] outputs the tangent of its input, an angle in radians. Unlike the signal object [cos~], which takes its input in cycles (0 to 1), the control-rate trigonometric functions use radians.

title: template

vanilla/template.body: [template] is the old name of [struct], which defines a data structure template and its fields. Use [struct] instead.

"text define" maintains a text object and can name it so that other objects can find it (and later should have some alternative, anonymous way to be found).

An optional -c flag allows you to read or write to/from a file interpreting carriage returns as separators.

The right outlet sends 0 if the line ended with a semicolon, 1 for a comma, or 2 if the number is out of range. The text is named by the argument or the right inlet, or found through a pointer with -s.

vanilla/text.body: [text] on its own is [text define], which creates a named text: a list of messages, separated by semicolons or commas, that other [text] objects can read and edit. Its first argument selects another function: get, set, insert, delete, size, tolist, fromlist, search or sequence. With -k, the contents are saved with the patch.

title: textfile

messages.description: output a whole line and go to the next
lines stored in the textfile object
when reaching the end of sequence

methods.description: add a message but don't terminate it
clear and add a message to textfile
write to a file (with optional 'cr' argument)

vanilla/textfile.body:
'cr' = terminating lines only with carriage return (omitting semicolons.) You can read files this way too, in which case carriage returns are mapped to semicolons.

The textfile object reads and writes text files to and from memory. You can read a file and output sequential lines as lists, or collect lines and write them out. You can use this object to generate "models" for Gem, for instance.

To record textual messages and save them to a file, first send "clear" to empty the qlist and "add" to add messages (terminated with semicolons.) The message, "add2" adds a list of atoms without finishing with a semicolon in case you want to make variable-length messages.

You can also use this object simply for storing heterogeneous sequences of lists.

title: tgl
toggle

methods.description: sets font type <0: DejaVu Sans Mono, 1: Helvetica, 2: Times> and font size
first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)
sets position in the patch canvas
changes the position by a x/y delta in pixels
zero sets to off, nonzero sets to on (no output)

vanilla/tgl.body: [tgl] is a toggle GUI: it alternates between 0 and a nonzero value (1 by default) when clicked or banged. A float sets the state and is passed through, 'set' sets it without output, and 'nonzero' sets the value used for on.

title: threshold~

messages.description: signal to analyze and trigger from
nonzero sets internal state to 'high', 'low' otherwise
bang when reaching or exceeding a trigger threshold
bang when receding below a rest threshold

methods.description: set different values for the 4 arguments

vanilla/threshold~.body: threshold~ monitors its input signal and outputs bangs when the signal reaches or exceeds a specified "trigger" value, and also when the signal recedes below a "rest" value - this is also known as a 'schmitt trigger'. You can specify debounce times in milliseconds for the threshold~ to wait after the two event types before triggering again.

title: throw~
vanilla/throw~.description: throw signal to a matching catch~ object

messages.description: signal to throw to a matching catch~ object

vanilla/throw~.body:
Any number of throw~ objects can add into one catch~ object (but two catch~ objects cannot share the same name.)

Note: the [throw~] objects have to be sorted before the [catch~] in the DSP chain, or else you'll never get less than a block's delay.

title: timer

methods.description: set tempo value (float) and time unit (symbol)

vanilla/timer.body: [timer] measures elapsed logical time: a bang in the left inlet resets it, and a bang in the right inlet outputs the time since then. Logical time moves forward as if all computation were instantaneous and every [delay] and [metro] were exact. Times are in milliseconds by default, which the 'tempo' message or the arguments can change.

title: touchin
vanilla/touchin.body: [touchin] outputs MIDI channel aftertouch values, with their channel. It listens on all channels by default; an argument sets the channel and removes the channel outlet. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: touchout
vanilla/touchout.body: [touchout] sends MIDI channel aftertouch values, on the channel set by the argument or the right inlet. Channels above 16 address further ports: 17 to 32 are channels 1 to 16 of port 2, and so on.

title: trace

messages.description: any message to be traced from this point on
arms the object for the given number of messages
bypasses the input message further down the chain

vanilla/trace.body: When 'set-tracing' is on and the object is armed,  trace prints in the Pd window the message it receives and also outputs the messages all the other objects further down in the chain send. You can control-click on the printout to select in the patch the object that caused the message. Once this is done,  trace also prints a backtrace of messages leading up to the one that has set it off.

title: trigger
t

messages.description: any message to be sequenced over the outlets
sequenced messages from right to left

arguments.description: symbols that define outlet's message type. 'float', 'bang', 'symbol', 'list', 'anything', and 'pointer', all of which can be abbreviated

vanilla/trigger.body: [trigger] sends its input to each of its outlets in right-to-left order, converting it as its arguments say: bang, float, symbol, list, anything, pointer, or a constant value.

title: unpack

messages.description: a list to be split into atoms
a float or a symbol, depending on the argument

vanilla/unpack.body: [unpack] splits a list into its elements and sends each out its own outlet, from right to left. The arguments set the number of outlets and the type of each element: f for float, s for symbol or p for pointer.

title: until

messages.description: set number of iterations in the loop

vanilla/until.body: The until object's left inlet starts a loop in which it outputs "bang" until its right inlet gets a bang which stops it. If you start "until" with a number,  it iterates at most that number of times,  as in the Max "uzi" object.

title: value
v
vanilla/value.description: share a number between objects by name

methods.description: sends the value to a matching receive name

vanilla/value.body:
"Value" stores a numeric value which is shared between all values with the same name (which need not be in the same Pd window.)

The value may also be stored or recalled in expressions via the expr, expr~, and fexpr~ objects.

The value object can also receive float values sent via a [send] object or a message if it has a variable with the same name.

title: vcf~
vanilla/vcf~.body:
Vcf~ is a resonant bandpass and lowpass filter that takes either a control or an audio signal to set center frequency, which may thus change continuously in time as in an analog voltage controlled filter (and unlike 'bp~' and 'lop~' that only take control values). The "Q" or filter sharpness is still only set by control messages.

Vcf~ is implemented as a one-pole complex filter with outlets for the real and imaginary value. These may be used as bandpass and lowpass filter outputs, or combined to allow other possibilities.

title: vline~

messages.description: set target value and start ramp
set next ramp time (cleared when ramp starts)

vanilla/vline~.body:
The vline~ object, like line~, generates linear ramps whose levels and timing are determined by messages you send it. It takes a target value, a time interval in milliseconds and an initial delay (also in ms). Ramps may start and stop between audio samples, in which case the output is interpolated accordingly.

A list up to three floats distributes the values over the inlets, as usual in Pd. Note that the middle and right inlet (that sets the time and delay) do not remember old values (unlike other inlets in Pd). Thus, if you send vline~ a float without priorly specifying a ramp time and delay and sent, it jumps immediately to the target value. In the same way, a list of two values will not have a delay time if no delay time was priorly set in the right inlet.

Any number of future ramps may be scheduled and vline~ will remember them and execute them in order. They must be specified in increasing order of initial delay however, since a segment cancels all planned segments at any future time.

!!! BUG: vline~ objects inside reblocked subpatches can have slightly incorrect timing !!!

title: vradio
vdl

methods.description: nonzero sets to vertical, zero sets to horizontal
sets font type <0: DejaVu Sans Mono, 1: Helvetica, 2: Times> and font size
first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)
sets position in the patch canvas
changes the position by a x/y delta in pixels

vanilla/vradio.body: [vradio] is a vertical radio button GUI: clicking one of its cells outputs that cell's number. Incoming floats set the value and are passed through, 'set' sets it without output, and a bang outputs it. Right click for properties such as the number of cells, size and colors.

title: vslider
vsl

methods.description: nonzero sets to vertical, zero sets to horizontal
sets font type <0: DejaVu Sans Mono, 1: Helvetica, 2: Times> and font size
first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)
sets position in the patch canvas
changes the position by a x/y delta in pixels
nonzero sets to steady, zero sets to jump on click

vanilla/vslider.body: [vslider] is a vertical slider GUI: click and drag to output values within its range, or shift-drag for fine tuning. Incoming floats set the value and are passed through, 'set' sets it without output, and a bang outputs it. Its scale can be linear or logarithmic.

title: vsnapshot~

messages.description: convert a signal to a float
the converted signal at every bang

vanilla/vsnapshot~.body:
mal-designed snapshot~ extension, best not to use this

This is an attempt at making a version of snapshot~ that trades off delay for time jitter control. The behaviour is the same as snapshot~ (it takes a bang and converts a signal to a float. The idea is that you can convert from an audio signal and get a specific value within an audio block depending on the exact time it receives a bang. Unfortunately it isn't fully correct and will be replaced by a more correct one in the future. Since this change will probably be incompatible with this object, it is probably best to avoid using it until it is working correctly.

title: vu

methods.description: nonzero shows scale (default), zero hides it

first element sets background color and third sets font color (either floats or symbols in hexadecimal format)

vanilla/vu.body: [vu] is a VU meter GUI that shows an RMS level (left inlet) and a peak level (right inlet) in dBFS; subtract 100 from what [env~] outputs to feed it. The values are passed on to the outlets.

title: wrap
vanilla/wrap.body: The wrap object wraps the input to a value between 0 and 1, including negative numbers (for instance, -0.2 maps to 0.8.)

title: wrap~
vanilla/wrap~.body: [wrap~] gives the difference between the input and the largest integer not exceeding it, which for positive numbers is the fractional part.

title: writesf~
vanilla/writesf~.description: write audio signals to a soundfile

messages.description: signal to write to a channel
signal to write to a channel

methods.description: prints information on Pd's terminal window

vanilla/writesf~.body:
writesf~ creates a subthread whose task is to write audio streams to disk. You need not provide any disk access time between "open" and "start", but between "stop" and the next "open" you must give the object time to flush all the output to disk.

The "open" message may take flag-style arguments as follows:

- -wave, -aiff, -caf, -next (file extension)
- -big, -little (sample endianness)
- -bytes <2, 3, or 4> (bit resolution)
- -rate <sample rate> (affects the soundfile header, but the file will not be resampled)

The soundfile is uncompressed 2- or 3-byte integer ("pcm") or 4-byte floating point. The soundfile format is determined by the file extension (e.g. "foo.wav", "foo.aiff", "foo.caf", "foo.snd").
